lessons.title: Ports and ephemeral allocation
lessons.summary: How port numbers let many programs share one IP address, and why a client's ephemeral port pool can run dry.
lessons.body:
IP delivers packets from one **host** to another. But a host can run many programs at once: a browser, a DNS resolver, an SSH session, a game. When a packet arrives, something has to decide which program gets it.

That is the transport layer's most basic job: **multiplexing** (many applications sharing one IP address on the way out) and **demultiplexing** (handing each arriving packet to the right application). The tool for it is the **port number**.

Two widely used Internet transports are TCP and UDP. Base **UDP** offers datagram boundaries, ports and a checksum, with few additional services. **TCP** adds a reliable, ordered byte stream with flow and congestion control. This module starts with UDP as a simple datagram transport; transport protocols need not all use the same multiplexing mechanism.

## Ports

A port is a 16-bit number, so 0 to 65,535. IANA splits the range into three bands:

| Range | Name | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 0–1023 | System (well-known) | 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS |
| 1024–49151 | User (registered) | 3306 MySQL, 5432 Postgres |
| 49152–65535 | Dynamic (ephemeral) | Client-side ports |

A server often **binds** to a known service port; discovery mechanisms can also advertise dynamically chosen ports. Port zero is reserved in the IANA registry, and asking a socket API to bind port zero typically requests automatic allocation. A client usually lets the OS pick a temporary **ephemeral port** for its end. Operating systems don't all follow the IANA range: Linux picks ephemeral ports from **32768–60999** by default (`net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`).

That default range holds 28,232 port numbers (both end points count). It is the most a client can draw on before reserved ports, ports already in use and configuration changes are considered.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Flat numbers in a block of flats
> A block of flats has one street address, but post is delivered to individual flats by number. A resident who sends a letter writes their own flat number on the envelope as the address for replies, so the answer comes back to the right door.
>
> **How it maps:** The IP address is the street address of the host; the port number is the flat number that picks one program on it. A server's well-known port is like a flat whose number is published; a client's ephemeral port is a temporary reply flat number the operating system picks for one conversation.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real flat numbers are permanent, whereas ephemeral ports are borrowed and later reused. The kernel also identifies a TCP conversation by both ends' addresses and ports together, not by the local port alone.

Why can the pool run dry? Picture a proxy that keeps opening short TCP connections from one source address to one backend address and port. Only its source port differs between those connections. If each used port stays unavailable for a while after the connection closes (later units explain why TCP holds it), the sustainable rate of new connections is at most the number of usable ports divided by that holding time. With the full Linux default range and a 60-second hold, that is roughly 470 new connections a second to that one backend. This is an explicit capacity model, not a promise about every operating system's reuse policy.

On Unix, binding to ports below 1024 traditionally needs root, the all-powerful administrator account (on Linux, typically `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, with the privileged-port threshold configurable per network namespace). That rule is a historical trust signal, not security.

## Key takeaways

- Ports distinguish transport endpoints; IANA service ranges and operating-system allocation policies are different concepts.
- The documented Linux ephemeral range contains 28,232 numbers before reservations and other constraints.
- Repeated short connections to one destination are limited by usable source ports divided by how long each port is held after closing.

## Further reading

- [RFC 6335: IANA port number procedures](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6335)
- [Ephemeral port — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemeral_port)
- [Linux IP sysctl defaults](https://kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/ip-sysctl.html)
- [RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768)

questions.prompt: A proxy uses one source IP and automatic source ports from Linux's default range (32768–60999). It opens many short TCP connections to one backend, 10.0.0.5:5432, and each used port stays unavailable for about 60 seconds after its connection closes. Above roughly 470 new connections a second, new attempts start failing because no local port is free. Which change directly raises that limit?

options.text: Increase the backend's listen() backlog
options.explanation: The backlog holds completed connections waiting for accept() on the backend. The failures here happen on the proxy, before any connection exists, because it has no free source port.

options.text: Move the backend from port 5432 to a higher port number such as 15432
options.explanation: The destination is still a single address and port, so every connection still differs only by source port. The number of usable tuples does not change.

options.text: Let the proxy use a second backend address (or a second source address) for the same service
options.explanation: Correct. Each new address/port combination gives the proxy another full set of distinct tuples, so the same pool of source ports can be reused against it (Linux's connect() does this; allocation policies differ on other systems). Connection pooling, which avoids most new connections, is the other standard fix.

options.text: Raise the TCP receive window on the proxy
options.explanation: The receive window controls how much data a peer may send on an existing connection. It has nothing to do with how many distinct connection tuples are available.

questions.workedExample:
1. Four of the five tuple fields are fixed: TCP, the proxy's IP, `10.0.0.5` and port 5432. Only the **source port** can differ between connections.
2. The pool is about 28,232 ports, and each one is held for about a minute after use, so the model allows roughly 28,232 ÷ 60 ≈ 470 new connections a second.
3. Anything that does not add distinct tuples or reduce the number of new connections leaves that ceiling where it is: the backend's backlog, its port number and window sizes are all irrelevant.
4. Adding another destination address (or source address) multiplies the available tuples. Reusing connections through a pool removes most of the demand. Widening the port range also helps, within limits.

lessons.title: UDP headers, checksums and payload limits
lessons.summary: UDP's eight-byte header, what its checksum does and does not protect, and why big datagrams are a bad idea.
lessons.body:
## The UDP header

UDP ([RFC 768](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768), 1980) is three pages long. Its header is 8 bytes:

```
 0      7 8     15 16    23 24    31
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|   Source port   |    Dest port    |
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|     Length      |    Checksum     |
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|        data (payload) ...         |
+-----------------------------------+
```

Four 16-bit fields make up the whole base header, so it is always 8 bytes:

- **Source port**: a reply-port hint when supplied; RFC 768 permits zero when unused. Application protocols can impose additional requirements.
- **Destination port**: which socket on the receiver gets this datagram.
- **Length**: header plus data, in bytes; at least 8 for an ordinary datagram. IPv6 jumbograms use the exception described below.
- **Checksum**: the 16-bit one's complement of the one's-complement sum over the header, the data and a **pseudo-header** of source IP, destination IP, protocol number and UDP length. Including addresses helps detect accidental misdelivery, but the checksum does not detect every error and provides no authentication.

The checksum is optional over IPv4 (a value of 0 means "not computed") and normally **required over IPv6**. RFC 6935/6936 permit narrowly constrained zero-checksum tunnel modes; ordinary IPv6 applications cannot simply disable it.

For ordinary UDP, the length field (16 bits) bounds header plus payload at 65,535 bytes. IPv6 jumbograms are a specified exception (RFC 2675), using UDP length zero when required.

Over IPv4 there is a second, tighter limit: the IPv4 header's own 16-bit total-length field counts the whole packet, IP header included. The IP header and the UDP header both come out of the same 65,535 bytes, so with a 20-byte IPv4 header the largest UDP payload is 65,535 − 20 − 8 = 65,507 bytes.

That is a protocol maximum, not a sensible size to send. An IP packet larger than the path MTU may be fragmented where allowed, rejected locally, or dropped with an ICMP error. On Linux (tested on kernel 6.12), a UDP socket's default path-MTU mode fragments an oversized datagram locally; a socket that sets `IP_PMTUDISC_DO` gets `EMSGSIZE` instead. IPv6 routers do not fragment. Reassembly needs all fragments, so UDP applications should manage payload sizes using path and protocol constraints rather than assume one universal safe size.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Postcards
> A postcard carries a destination address, an optional sender's address and the message. The postal service makes no promise that it arrives, arrives once, or arrives before the card you sent the next day, and you are not told if it is lost.
>
> **How it maps:** A UDP datagram is a self-contained postcard: the ports and IP addresses are the addresses, and each `sendto()` produces one card that arrives whole or not at all. There is no conversation to set up first.
>
> **Where it stops:** UDP's checksum lets the receiver detect some corruption and discard the card, which the post office does not do. A postcard has no size limit tied to the road it travels; a large datagram may have to be split into IP fragments, and losing any one of them loses the whole datagram.

> [!note] What UDP does not do
> Base UDP provides no handshake, acknowledgements, retransmission, ordering, flow control or congestion control. Datagrams may be lost, duplicated or reordered. Ordinary datagram socket calls preserve message boundaries; a too-small receive buffer can truncate a message and discard its remainder. A successful send is not proof of remote delivery.

RFC 9868 (October 2025) defines UDP transport options after the user-data area; it does not enlarge the base eight-byte header. This lesson describes ordinary datagrams without those options or socket segmentation/coalescing extensions.

## Key takeaways

- The base UDP header has four 16-bit fields and occupies eight bytes.
- Checksums help detect corruption without authenticating the sender; ordinary IPv6 UDP normally requires one.
- The IPv4 maximum payload is 65,507 bytes with minimal headers; path constraints usually require much smaller datagrams.

## Further reading

- [RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768)
- [User Datagram Protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_Datagram_Protocol)
- [RFC 6935: IPv6 UDP checksum exceptions](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6935)
- [RFC 2675: IPv6 jumbograms](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2675)
- [RFC 9868: UDP transport options](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9868)
- [Linux UDP socket semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/udp.7.html)

questions.prompt: A capture shows a UDP header of 8 bytes, while the TCP segments on the same host have headers of at least 20 bytes. What best explains the difference?

options.text: UDP compresses its header fields, while TCP sends them uncompressed
options.explanation: Neither protocol compresses its header. UDP's header is small because it has fewer fields, not because the same fields are encoded more tightly.

options.text: Base UDP promises no ordering, retransmission or flow control, so it needs no sequence, acknowledgement or window fields
options.explanation: Correct. UDP carries only source port, destination port, length and checksum: four 16-bit fields. TCP's extra fields exist to support the services it promises.

options.text: UDP leaves out port numbers and relies on the IP header to choose the application
options.explanation: UDP does carry source and destination ports; IP has no field that selects an application. Ports are half of UDP's header.

options.text: UDP has no checksum, which saves the bytes TCP spends on one
options.explanation: UDP has a 16-bit checksum. It is optional over IPv4 but normally required over IPv6.

questions.workedExample:
1. List what each header must support. UDP delivers a datagram to a port and lets the receiver check for some corruption: that needs two ports, a length and a checksum.
2. Four 16-bit fields are 64 bits, which is 8 bytes.
3. TCP additionally promises an ordered, reliable, flow-controlled byte stream, so its header carries a sequence number, an acknowledgement number, flags and a window, which bring it to 20 bytes before options.
4. The header size follows directly from the services each protocol promises.

questions.prompt: An application sends one 60,000-byte UDP datagram over IPv4 across Ethernet links with a 1,500-byte MTU. Which outcome should it expect?

options.text: The send is always rejected, because 60,000 bytes exceeds UDP's maximum payload
options.explanation: The IPv4 limit for one UDP payload is 65,507 bytes with a 20-byte IP header, so 60,000 bytes is within the protocol maximum. Practical path limits are a separate problem.

options.text: UDP splits the data into about 41 separate datagrams, which the receiving application reads one by one
options.explanation: UDP never splits a datagram into several datagrams. Any splitting happens at the IP layer as fragments, and the receiving application sees either the whole datagram or nothing.

options.text: The network automatically switches the transfer to TCP to make it reliable
options.explanation: Nothing in UDP or IP switches transports. Applications such as DNS may retry over TCP themselves, but that is application logic.

options.text: Depending on the socket's path-MTU settings it is either refused locally or sent as IP fragments; if fragmented, losing any one fragment loses the whole datagram
options.explanation: Correct. The datagram cannot fit in one 1,500-byte packet. By default Linux fragments it locally; a socket that sets the Don't Fragment (DF) flag on every packet with IP_PMTUDISC_DO gets EMSGSIZE instead. Where fragmentation is allowed, every fragment must arrive for reassembly, and UDP does not retransmit.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare the datagram with the protocol limit: 60,000 bytes is below the 65,507-byte IPv4 maximum, so UDP itself can describe it.
2. Compare it with the path: one Ethernet packet carries at most 1,500 bytes, so the datagram cannot travel as a single packet.
3. Two things can then happen. The sending host may refuse it (Linux returns `EMSGSIZE` when the socket sets the Don't Fragment (DF) flag with `IP_PMTUDISC_DO`), or IP may split it (Linux's default socket mode does this) into fragments of up to 1,480 bytes of IP payload each.
4. If fragmented, the receiver can only reassemble it when **every** fragment arrives. One lost fragment loses the whole datagram, and UDP will not resend it.
5. That is why UDP applications keep datagrams small, for example DNS's 1,232-byte guidance.

questions.prompt: Which facilities does base UDP provide, without higher-level reliability protocols? Select all that apply.

options.text: Delivery to the right application via port numbers
options.explanation: Correct. UDP uses port fields to support application demultiplexing; not every possible transport protocol must use UDP-style ports.

options.text: Detection of corrupted datagrams via a checksum
options.explanation: Correct. When enabled and verified, the checksum detects some corruption, including in the pseudo-header. It does not detect all errors or authenticate the sender, and IPv4 permits omission.

options.text: Retransmission of lost datagrams
options.explanation: UDP never retransmits. If an application needs reliability (as DNS resolvers do), it must implement timeouts and retries itself.

options.text: Preservation of message boundaries
options.explanation: Correct for ordinary UDP socket use. Received datagrams remain separate; too-small buffers can truncate a datagram, and successful sending does not guarantee delivery.

options.text: In-order delivery
options.explanation: Base UDP does not specify ordered delivery or receive-side resequencing. Applications can add their own sequence information and ordering policy.

questions.workedExample: Base UDP defines source/destination ports, a datagram length and a checksum. These support demultiplexing, message boundaries and limited error detection. It does not define ordered delivery or automatic loss recovery. Protocol guarantees follow from the specification and state machine, not merely from whether a similarly named header field exists.

lessons.title: UDP sockets and TCP connection tuples
lessons.summary: How the kernel hands each arriving packet to the right socket: destination port for UDP, the full connection tuple for TCP.
lessons.body:
## Demultiplexing: sockets and 5-tuples

An application talks to the transport layer through a **socket**. The kernel needs a rule for choosing which socket an arriving packet belongs to. UDP and TCP use different rules.

## UDP: match on the destination

An unconnected IPv4 UDP socket bound to `0.0.0.0:53` can receive datagrams addressed to port 53 across local IPv4 addresses. Filtering, competing specific/reuse bindings, multicast membership and implementation rules can affect delivery. A DNS server can use one bound UDP socket for requests from many different client endpoints, reading each sender's address from `recvfrom()`.

```python
import socket

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,
                  socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9999))
while True:
    # Each read consumes one datagram.
    data, addr = s.recvfrom(2048)
    # Reply to this datagram's sender.
    s.sendto(data.upper(), addr)
```

The echo example binds loopback and truncates received datagrams above 2,048 bytes; it is a small demonstration, not a production service.

Calling `connect()` on a UDP socket establishes a default peer and normally restricts received datagrams to it. It performs no UDP handshake; route lookup or neighbour resolution and socket error handling can still occur. API details, including whether explicit sends to other destinations are permitted, vary.

## TCP: match on the full 5-tuple

A TCP connection is identified by its **5-tuple**:

```
(protocol, src IP, src port,
           dst IP, dst port)
```

A web server listening on port 443 has one listening socket, plus one **accepted socket per TCP connection**. Two separate connections from one client address can differ in source port; browser tabs can also share pooled connections:

```
TCP 198.51.100.7:51000 -> 203.0.113.5:443
TCP 198.51.100.7:51001 -> 203.0.113.5:443
```

Both arrive at the same server port, but they differ in one field, so they are different connections. This is why a server can handle hundreds of thousands of connections on a single port: capacity depends on resources such as memory, file descriptors, CPU and distinct connection tuples; one server port does not impose a 65,535-connection total limit.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: One restaurant door, many tables
> Every party enters a restaurant through the same front door. The host greets each party and seats it at its own table, and from then on the waiter serves each table separately.
>
> **How it maps:** The front door is the listening socket on port 443; the host is `accept()`, which hands back a new socket for each connection. Each table is an accepted socket, and the kernel finds the right table for an arriving segment by the full tuple: who the guests are (client address and port) as well as which door they used.
>
> **Where it stops:** A restaurant runs out of tables quickly, whereas a server's limit comes from memory, file descriptors and CPU. And UDP has no host at all: an unconnected UDP socket is a single counter where every datagram for that port lands, whoever sent it.

> [!example] Ephemeral port exhaustion
> A client connects repeatedly to one backend, `10.0.0.5:5432`. Four of the five fields are fixed; only the source port varies. With Linux's default range, with a single fixed source address and automatic allocation confined to that range, at most 28,232 distinct local ports are available before other reservations and constraints. TIME_WAIT can further restrict tuple reuse (the connection-management units). Proxies hit this; fixes are connection pooling, extra source IPs, or more backend IPs.

## Key takeaways

- An unconnected UDP socket can receive messages from multiple senders; UDP connect does not perform a handshake.
- Accepted TCP connections share a listening port and are distinguished by their connection tuples.
- A UDP receive buffer that is too small can truncate a datagram rather than save its remainder for another read.

## Further reading

- [Linux UDP socket semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/udp.7.html)
- [RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768)
- [Ephemeral port — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemeral_port)

questions.prompt:
On localhost, a UDP client runs:

```python
# Each send is one datagram.
s.sendto(b"a" * 100, srv)
s.sendto(b"b" * 200, srv)
s.sendto(b"c" * 300, srv)
```

The server loops on `data, _ = s.recvfrom(2048)` and prints `len(data)`. Assuming ordinary datagram socket calls, no loss, duplication or reordering, what does it print?

options.explanation: That is what a TCP receiver might see, since TCP is a byte stream and can merge writes. UDP never merges datagrams.

options.text: `100`, `200`, `300` on separate lines
options.explanation: Correct. UDP preserves message boundaries: three `sendto()` calls produce three datagrams, and each `recvfrom()` returns exactly one.

options.text: `2048` three times
options.explanation: The 2048 is the buffer size, the maximum the call will return. `recvfrom` returns the actual datagram length.

options.text: It depends on how the kernel chooses to split the data
options.explanation: Ordinary UDP sockets preserve datagram boundaries. Here the buffer is large enough; smaller receive buffers can truncate a message rather than return it whole.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each `sendto()` builds one UDP datagram with its own length field: 100, 200, 300 bytes of payload.
2. The receiver's kernel queues each datagram as a separate unit.
3. Each `recvfrom(2048)` dequeues one datagram. The buffer is big enough, so nothing is truncated.
4. Output:

```
100
200
300
```

Two caveats: over a real network the order could change or one could vanish; and if the buffer were smaller than a datagram (say `recvfrom(50)`), the excess would be **discarded**, not saved for the next call.

questions.prompt: An HTTPS service accepts 100,000 simultaneous TCP connections on one server IP and local port 443. How many distinct local TCP port numbers do those accepted sockets use?

options.text: 100,000, one per client
options.explanation: The server does not allocate a new port per client. Each accepted connection gets a new socket, but it shares the listening port.

options.text: At most 65,535, so it cannot have 100,000 clients
options.explanation: This confuses the port space with the connection space. Connections are identified by 5-tuples, of which there are vastly more than 65,535.

options.text: About 28,000, the size of the ephemeral range
options.explanation: These accepted sockets retain the listener’s local port. The initiating endpoint may choose an ephemeral source port or explicitly bind one.

options.text: One: port 443, with connections told apart by the client's IP and port
options.explanation: Correct. All connections have destination port 443; the kernel demultiplexes them by the full 5-tuple, in which the client's address and port differ.

questions.workedExample:
1. Every client connects to `server_ip:443`.
2. On the server, `accept()` returns a new socket for each connection, but that socket's local address is still `server_ip:443`.
3. The kernel tells them apart by the 5-tuple:

```
(TCP, c1_ip, c1_port, srv, 443)
(TCP, c2_ip, c2_port, srv, 443)
...
```

4. So the server uses one port. Practical limits include memory, file descriptors, CPU and connection-tuple availability; this question specifies a service using just one local port.

lessons.title: Choosing UDP for DNS
lessons.summary: Why DNS asks its questions over UDP, and what happens when an answer is too big.
lessons.body:
## Why would anyone choose UDP?

TCP gives you reliability and ordering, but you pay in **latency** (a normal new-connection handshake and possible waits for retransmissions; extensions and connection reuse change this cost) and **control** (the kernel decides when to send and what to wait for). UDP is right when one of those costs is unacceptable.

## DNS: one question, one answer

A DNS lookup is usually a single small query and a single small response. With UDP the whole exchange takes **one round trip**. A fresh ordinary TCP connection adds a handshake; an already open connection can be reused, and TCP Fast Open can alter setup timing. Total resolution latency also includes DNS processing and any upstream queries.

Reliability is handled by the application: if no reply arrives within a timeout, the resolver asks again or tries another server. If a response is too big for UDP, the server sets the **TC (truncated)** flag and the client retries over TCP. EDNS(0) allows UDP responses bigger than the original 512-byte limit; DNS Flag Day 2020 recommended a 1,232-byte UDP payload limit. The number comes from the smallest packet every IPv6 link must carry: 1,280 bytes, minus the 40-byte base IPv6 header and the 8-byte UDP header, leaves 1,232 bytes. A DNS message of that size fits in one packet on any IPv6 path when no extra headers or tunnels are added.

This reduces fragmentation risk under those assumptions rather than proving every path can carry it.

## Key takeaways

- A small DNS query/response can use one UDP round trip, with application retry policy supplying recovery.
- A truncated DNS response prompts TCP retry; EDNS advertises a larger UDP capacity.
- The 1,232-byte recommendation follows from minimal IPv6/UDP headers and the 1,280-byte IPv6 minimum MTU, with stated path assumptions.

## Further reading

- [DNS Flag Day 2020 guidance](https://www.dnsflagday.net/2020/)
- [RFC 8085: UDP Usage Guidelines](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085)

questions.prompt: A resolver sends a DNS query over UDP. The answer is too large for the UDP size the server is willing to send. What happens in standard DNS?

options.text: The server sends a truncated reply with the TC flag set, and the client retries the query over TCP
options.explanation: Correct for this standard truncation/retry path. DNS-over-TCP supports larger messages, but still uses a two-byte message-length field; it is not unlimited.

options.text: The server fragments the response into several UDP datagrams and the client reassembles them
options.explanation: DNS has no application-level reassembly of UDP replies. IP fragmentation can occur, but it is exactly what DNS tries to avoid.

options.text: The server silently drops the query
options.explanation: The server does answer: it marks the reply as truncated so the client knows to retry.

options.text: UDP automatically switches to TCP mode
options.explanation: UDP has no such mode. The switch to TCP is done by the DNS client, prompted by the TC flag.

questions.workedExample:
1. Original UDP DNS used a 512-byte limit; EDNS lets a requester advertise a larger UDP payload size.
2. DNS Flag Day 2020 recommended 1,232 bytes to reduce fragmentation risk under IPv6 minimum-MTU/header assumptions.
3. A truncated response sets TC; the resolver can retry using TCP as specified by DNS handling rules.
4. A new TCP connection adds handshake cost; a reusable connection changes that timing. DNS-over-TCP messages still have a 65,535-byte length-field limit.

lessons.title: Real-time updates and transport over UDP
lessons.summary: Why games, calls and QUIC use UDP: fresh data matters more than waiting for old data.
lessons.body:
## Live games and voice: old data is useless

Consider a game sending independent full-state position snapshots 60 times a second: one every 16.7 ms or so. A 100 ms stall therefore spans about six snapshots, and by the time a lost one could be resent, several newer ones already describe the world better.

A new snapshot can supersede a lost one; delta updates and important game events can have different reliability requirements. TCP would **hold back** every later update until the lost one was retransmitted, delaying delivery of later bytes until the gap is repaired. The delay depends on detection, retransmission and buffering; the whole game loop need not freeze. That is **head-of-line blocking**, and independent deadline-sensitive updates can prefer skipping out-of-date data to waiting for that gap.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A live scoreboard by text message
> A friend texts you the score of a match every minute. If one text goes missing, you do not want them to resend "2–1 at 63 minutes" when you already have "3–1 at 64 minutes"; and you certainly would not want your phone to hide the newer texts until the old one turned up.
>
> **How it maps:** Each text is an independent snapshot of the whole game state sent in a UDP datagram, which the game can simply skip when it is superseded. TCP behaves like a phone that refuses to show later texts until the missing one is redelivered: that is head-of-line blocking.
>
> **Where it stops:** Some game messages are not superseded, such as "player picked up the key", and need their own reliability. Real-time media also has hard playback deadlines, so late audio may be concealed rather than simply skipped.

Voice and video calls (RTP over UDP) work the same way: a late frame may be concealed or discarded, but timely retransmission and forward error correction can also help. RFC 4588 specifies RTP retransmission; media deadlines determine its usefulness.

## QUIC: build your own transport

QUIC ([RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)), the transport under HTTP/3, uses UDP; HTTP/3 commonly uses **port 443**, but QUIC is not restricted to that port. QUIC provides its own loss recovery, stream reliability, congestion control and protected transport, and can be implemented in user space. UDP is used not because QUIC wants unreliability, but because using existing UDP socket support can ease endpoint and middlebox deployment. UDP is neither the only permitted non-TCP transport nor guaranteed to pass every path. The transport-performance units cover why.

## Others

Examples using UDP include DHCPv4 initial discovery, conventional NTP/SNMP exchanges, UDP syslog, multicast media and WireGuard. Several of these application families also define other transports; “syslog” alone does not imply UDP.

## Key takeaways

- Independent state updates can supersede old data, while important events may need separate reliability.
- TCP delivery gaps can delay later stream bytes; this need not freeze an entire game loop.
- QUIC builds protected, congestion-controlled transport services above UDP rather than relying on base UDP for reliability.

## Further reading

- [RFC 4588: RTP retransmission](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4588)
- [RFC 8085: UDP Usage Guidelines](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085)
- [User Datagram Protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_Datagram_Protocol)

questions.prompt: Which requirements can motivate an application to use ordinary UDP datagrams with application-specific control instead of one TCP byte stream? This compares base transports, not reliable protocols such as QUIC built above UDP. Select all that apply.

options.text: Independent full-state game snapshots where superseded updates should not block newer ones
options.explanation: Correct. The application can discard stale snapshots and avoid TCP byte-stream head-of-line blocking. Important events or delta-dependent state may require separate reliability.

options.text: A software download whose only stated requirement is reliable delivery of every file byte
options.explanation: That requirement alone does not motivate replacing TCP with base UDP. A higher-level reliable protocol such as QUIC can also carry downloads; this is not a claim that files cannot use UDP-based transports.

options.text: A small DNS request/reply where avoiding a fresh transport handshake is useful
options.explanation: Correct. UDP can carry the small exchange without a transport handshake; DNS still needs retries, validation and TCP support where required. Existing TCP connections can be reused.

options.text: Deadline-sensitive voice packets for which later packets should not wait for expired ones
options.explanation: Correct. Media-specific loss recovery can respect playback deadlines. Concealment, FEC or timely retransmission can all be useful; retransmission is not universally pointless.

options.text: A payment API whose only stated requirement is that the transaction must not be lost
options.explanation: Base UDP adds no delivery guarantee. TCP or QUIC can carry reliable data, but neither alone guarantees durable payment processing: acknowledgements, retries and idempotency belong at the application layer.

questions.workedExample: Select the requirements that benefit from independent datagrams or no fresh transport handshake: snapshots, a small DNS exchange and deadline-sensitive voice. A file’s completeness requirement or a payment’s durability requirement alone does not motivate bare UDP. Reliable transports built over UDP remain valid options, and application correctness is separate from byte delivery.

questions.prompt: A game sends 60 small position updates per second to the server over **TCP**. RTT is 100 ms. One segment carrying an update is lost. What does the server's game loop experience?

options.text: It misses that one update and carries on with the next one 16 ms later
options.explanation: TCP does not skip missing stream bytes to expose later ones. UDP-based independent snapshots can avoid that stream-ordering constraint, subject to loss and scheduling.

options.text: Nothing at all, because TCP retransmits transparently
options.explanation: The retransmission is transparent to correctness, not to timing. The delay it causes is the whole problem.

options.text: Later bytes on that TCP stream wait for the missing bytes; after recovery, several buffered updates may become readable
options.explanation: Correct. TCP exposes an ordered byte stream. The question’s RTT does not specify an exact stall duration or imply the application’s whole game loop freezes.

options.text: The TCP connection is reset
options.explanation: One lost segment does not by itself instruct TCP to reset. Recovery is normally attempted; repeated failure can eventually reach an implementation or application timeout.

questions.workedExample:
1. Later stream bytes can arrive out of order and be buffered by the receiving TCP.
2. TCP cannot expose them to the application until the earlier gap is filled.
3. Loss detection and recovery time depend on ACKs, timers, the loss position and the implementation, so the RTT alone gives no exact pause length.
4. For a sense of scale: updates 60 times a second are about 16.7 ms apart, so a 100 ms round trip spans about six of them. That is an illustration, not a guaranteed six-update stall.
5. When the gap fills, several buffered updates become readable at once. The application can keep running local prediction or other work while it waits.

questions.prompt: Why does QUIC run on top of UDP rather than as a brand-new IP protocol alongside TCP and UDP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using existing UDP support can ease traversal of middleboxes compared with introducing a new IP protocol number
options.explanation: Correct. Some devices filter unknown protocols or lack suitable translation support. Devices can support other transports too, and UDP can itself be blocked.

options.text: UDP lets QUIC be implemented in an application or library in user space, without waiting for OS kernels to be updated
options.explanation: Correct. Existing UDP socket interfaces allow QUIC implementations in application libraries; operating-system policy and network access still apply.

options.text: UDP provides the reliability QUIC needs, so QUIC doesn't have to implement it
options.explanation: UDP provides no reliability. QUIC implements acknowledgements, retransmission and congestion control itself.

options.text: UDP's checksum replaces the need for encryption
options.explanation: The checksum is not cryptographic authentication. QUIC uses TLS 1.3 for its handshake and derives keys for packet protection; a checksum does not replace that.

questions.workedExample:
1. Reusing UDP allows implementations to use existing endpoint socket APIs and network support.
2. This can reduce the deployment changes required by a new IP protocol.
3. It does not make UDP universally reachable or restrict QUIC to user-space implementations.
4. QUIC supplies its own loss recovery, stream ordering, congestion control and packet protection above UDP.

lessons.title: Congestion, reflection and UDP deployment
lessons.summary: The duties UDP leaves to the application: congestion control, reflection attacks, NAT timeouts and fragmentation.
lessons.body:
## Pitfalls of UDP

- **You own congestion control.** UDP will happily send faster than the network can carry, hurting everyone. [RFC 8085](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085) requires applications to account for congestion and describes suitable control or rate-limiting behaviour for different traffic patterns; low-volume applications are not universally exempt.
- **Amplification attacks.** With no handshake, an attacker can spoof a victim's source address and send small queries to open servers that reply with much bigger responses. Cloudflare documented large amplification from exposed Memcached UDP services in 2018. Amplification depends on the request, stored response and counting of protocol overhead; the attack does not follow merely from choosing UDP.
- **NAT and firewalls.** Idle mapping lifetimes vary. RFC 4787 specifies a normal minimum of two minutes, with a defined exception for some well-known destination ports; actual equipment may differ. Applications needing inbound reachability must account for the relevant timeout and keepalive policy. Some corporate networks block UDP outright, so clients supporting HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 can fall back to TCP; a QUIC-only application has no automatic TCP fallback.
- **Fragmentation.** Oversized datagrams may fail locally or require permitted fragmentation. Fragment loss or filtering can prevent reassembly; UDP does not retransmit the missing data.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Catalogue requests in someone else's name
> A prankster fills in hundreds of free postcards asking companies to post a heavy catalogue, writing a neighbour's address as the sender's address. Each postcard is light, but the neighbour's doormat is buried under catalogues.
>
> **How it maps:** The postcards are small spoofed UDP queries; the companies are open servers that reply without checking who asked; the catalogues are much larger responses, all delivered to the victim whose address was forged. The size ratio is the amplification factor.
>
> **Where it stops:** Network traffic arrives in seconds rather than days, and many networks can filter forged source addresses before they leave. Some UDP-based protocols also limit replies to an address they have not validated; QUIC, for example, caps a server at three times the bytes it has received until the client's address is validated.

## Key takeaways

- UDP applications must account for congestion; choosing datagrams does not remove network responsibility.
- Spoofed requests and large open-server replies can create reflection amplification.
- Mapping lifetimes, fragmentation and UDP reachability vary across paths and deployments.

## Further reading

- [RFC 8085: UDP Usage Guidelines](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085)
- [Memcrashed: amplification attacks from port 11211 — Cloudflare blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/memcrashed-major-amplification-attacks-from-port-11211/)
- [User Datagram Protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_Datagram_Protocol)

questions.prompt: An attacker controls machines that send 100 Mbit/s of UDP queries to open servers, with each query's source address forged to be a victim's IP. Each reply is 50 times bigger than the query that caused it. Assume no source-address filtering, rate limiting or capacity limits. Why does this work, and roughly how much traffic reaches the victim?

options.text: It works because UDP has no checksum; about 100 Mbit/s
options.explanation: UDP does have a checksum, and it is irrelevant here. The trick is the forged source, and the replies are bigger than the queries.

options.text: It works because TCP SYN cookies are disabled; about 5 Gbit/s
options.explanation: SYN cookies are a TCP defence and have nothing to do with UDP. The figure is right but the mechanism is wrong.

options.text: It can't work: the replies go back to the attacker's machines
options.explanation: Replies go to whatever address is in the source field. With a forged source, that is the victim.

options.text: UDP has no handshake, so the servers reply to the forged address; each reply is 50 times larger, so about 5 Gbit/s
options.explanation: Correct under the assumptions. Nothing in UDP checks that the sender owns its source address, and the servers multiply every query byte by 50 on its way to the victim.

questions.workedExample:
1. The servers cannot tell that the source address is forged: UDP has no handshake that would prove the requester can receive replies at that address.
2. So every reply is sent to the victim, not to the attacker.
3. Each reply is 50 times the size of its query, so 100 Mbit/s of queries becomes about 50 × 100 Mbit/s = 5 Gbit/s arriving at the victim, while the attacker never sees any of it.
4. Defences include source-address filtering by networks, response rate limiting, and protocols that validate the requester's address before sending large replies. TCP's handshake changes the attack surface but does not make every reflection or denial-of-service attack impossible.

lessons.title: Reading the TCP handshake
lessons.summary: How SYN, SYN+ACK and ACK set up two sequence spaces, and why SYN and FIN each use up one number.
lessons.body:
TCP offers a **reliable, ordered byte stream** between two endpoints. Normal establishment synchronises sequence spaces and checks bidirectional reachability; this is not cryptographic peer authentication. Data can accompany handshake segments, and extensions such as TCP Fast Open can allow early application delivery. Graceful closure acknowledges the byte stream in each direction, not application processing or durable storage of those bytes. That bookkeeping is **connection management**.

The rules come from RFC 793 (1981), now consolidated in [RFC 9293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293) (2022).

## The TCP header, briefly

The fields that matter for connection management:

- **Sequence number** (32 bits): the first sequence-space position in the segment; a SYN occupies its own position before any data.
- **Acknowledgement number** (32 bits): the next byte the sender expects to receive. Only valid when the ACK flag is set.
- **Flags**: `SYN` (synchronise sequence numbers), `ACK`, `FIN` (no more data from me), `RST` (abort), plus `PSH`, `URG`, `ECE`, `CWR`.
- **Window** (16 bits): flow control (the flow-control units).
- **Options**: MSS, window scale, SACK-permitted, timestamps. MSS, window scale and SACK permission are exchanged on SYN segments. Negotiated timestamps accompany later segments, and SACK blocks can appear on later ACKs.

The header is 20 bytes without options and at most 60 with them. The limit comes from the 4-bit **data offset** field, which gives the header length in 4-byte words: its largest value, 15, means 60 bytes, leaving at most 40 bytes for options after the 20 fixed bytes.

That 40-byte option budget is small, and options compete for it (the SACK unit shows SACK running into it).

## The three-way handshake

Each side picks an **initial sequence number** (ISN). The handshake exchanges and acknowledges both:

```
Client                       Server
  |  SYN seq=1000              |
  |--------------------------->|
  |                            |
  |  SYN+ACK seq=5000 ack=1001 |
  |<---------------------------|
  |                            |
  |  ACK seq=1001 ack=5001     |
  |--------------------------->|
  |  (data can now flow)       |
```

Two rules make the numbers work:

1. **SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number**, independently of any data carried in the same segment. That is why the server acknowledges 1001, not 1000.
2. The cumulative ACK identifies the next expected sequence-space position in that direction, going back to 0 after 4,294,967,296 positions (the modulo arithmetic is explained below). It acknowledges contiguous received stream data/control positions, not successful application processing.

Applied to the trace above, rule 1 explains every number: the client's SYN uses 1000, so its first data byte will be 1001 and the server acknowledges 1001; the server's SYN uses 5000, so the client acknowledges 5001.

The wraparound in rule 2 occurs because the sequence number is a 32-bit field. Arithmetic on it wraps round like a clock: after the largest 32-bit value, 4,294,967,295, comes 0 again. The general rule for where the next segment starts is:

```formula reference
N_next = (N + L) mod 2^32
where
N_next: the sequence number just after a segment: the ACK number that acknowledges it
N: the segment's sequence number (its first position)
L: how many sequence numbers the segment uses: its data bytes, plus 1 for a SYN and 1 for a FIN
mod: modulo, the remainder after dividing; "mod 2^32" divides by 4,294,967,296 (32 twos multiplied together) and keeps the remainder, so totals wrap back into the range 0 to 4,294,967,295
In words: the next sequence number is the segment's first number plus the data bytes it carries, plus one for a SYN and one for a FIN, wrapping back to 0 after 4,294,967,295.
```

The final ACK may carry data itself; clients often send the HTTP request or TLS ClientHello right behind it.

## Key takeaways

- The handshake exchanges and acknowledges both initial sequence numbers.
- Each SYN or FIN consumes one sequence position; ordinary ACK-only segments do not.
- Sequence arithmetic wraps at the end of the 32-bit space, and an ACK does not certify application processing.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)

questions.prompt: A client sends a SYN at sequence number 1000. The server replies a SYN+ACK at sequence number 5000, acknowledging 1001. What are the sequence and acknowledgement numbers in the client's final ACK of the handshake? Assume neither SYN carries payload and there is no earlier data transmission.

options.explanation: This forgets that a SYN consumes one sequence number. The client's SYN used 1000, so its next byte is 1001; the server's SYN used 5000, so the client expects 5001 next.
The sequence number is right, but ack=5000 would claim the server's SYN hasn't been received yet. The ACK names the next byte expected, which is 5001.
Correct. The client's SYN consumed 1000, so it continues at 1001. The server's SYN consumed 5000, so the client acknowledges with 5001, meaning 'send me byte 5001 next'.
This swaps the two sequence spaces. Each direction has its own numbering: the client sends in its own space (starting at 1000) and acknowledges the server's (starting at 5000).

questions.workedExample:
1. Each direction has its own sequence space. The client's ISN is 1000; the server's is 5000.
2. **A SYN consumes one sequence number**, even with no data. The client's SYN occupies 1000, so the client's next number is **1001**, which matches the server's `ack=1001`.
3. The server's SYN occupies 5000. The client has received it, so the next server number it wants is **5001**.
4. The final segment is therefore:

```
ACK seq=1001 ack=5001
```

If the client puts data in this segment (say a TLS ClientHello), its first data byte is numbered 1001.

questions.prompt: After the handshake, a client's next sequence number is 1001. It sends 300 bytes of data in one segment and then sends FIN. What is the FIN's sequence number, and what ACK number does the server send to acknowledge the FIN?

options.text: FIN seq=1300, ACK 1301
options.explanation: Off by one. 300 bytes starting at 1001 occupy 1001 to 1300 inclusive, so the next number, used by the FIN, is 1301.

options.text: FIN seq=1301, ACK 1301
options.explanation: The FIN's sequence number is right, but a FIN consumes a sequence number of its own, so acknowledging it means asking for 1302.

options.text: FIN seq=1301, ACK 1302
options.explanation: Correct. The data takes 1001 to 1300, the FIN takes 1301, and the server's ACK names the next number it expects: 1302.

options.text: FIN seq=1001, ACK 1002
options.explanation: This treats the FIN as if no data had been sent. The 300 data bytes advance the sequence number by 300 first.

questions.workedExample:
1. The 300 data bytes start at 1001, so they occupy 1001 up to and including 1300 (the first byte counts, so the last is one less than 1001 + 300).
2. The server acknowledges the data with `ack=1301`: the next number it expects.
3. The FIN takes the next number: sequence number **1301**.
4. Like a SYN, a FIN **consumes one sequence number**, so the server acknowledges it with **1302**.

This is why a peer can tell 'I have all your data' (acknowledgement 1301) apart from 'I have all your data **and** your FIN' (acknowledgement 1302).

lessons.title: Stale handshakes and unpredictable ISNs
lessons.summary: Why the handshake needs three messages, and why initial sequence numbers must be hard to guess.
lessons.body:
## Why three messages, not two?

Each side must learn that the **other** side received its ISN. The client's SYN is acknowledged by the server's SYN+ACK; the server's SYN is acknowledged by the client's final ACK. Two messages would leave the server not knowing whether its ISN arrived.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Starting a call on a bad line
> On a crackly phone line, you say "Can you hear me?" The other person says "Yes, I can hear you; can you hear me?" You answer "Yes." Only after the third message do both of you know that speech gets through in both directions.
>
> **How it maps:** The first question is the client's SYN, the reply that both confirms and asks is the SYN+ACK, and your final "yes" is the ACK. Each side's starting sequence number is like the first thing it said, and each side needs the other to confirm it arrived.
>
> **Where it stops:** Hearing a voice tells you who is speaking; a TCP handshake does not prove the server's identity, which is TLS's job. TCP also numbers its "words" and must reject delayed copies of an old call, which a phone conversation never has to do.

There is also the **old duplicate** problem. A SYN delayed in the network from a long-dead attempt could arrive at the server. With three messages, the server's SYN+ACK reaches a client that is not expecting it, and the client replies with RST. If that response arrives, the server abandons the stale attempt. With no reply, it can retain half-open state until timeout; the handshake is not a defence against every spoof or replay scenario.

## Why random ISNs?

If ISNs were predictable (say, always 0), two problems arise:

- **Stale segments**: a delayed segment from a previous connection with the same 5-tuple could fall inside the new connection's sequence space and be accepted as data.
- **Spoofing**: an off-path attacker who can guess the server's ISN can forge the final ACK and inject data while pretending to be another IP. Predictable sequence numbers have historically enabled off-path spoofing; reachability and other validation assumptions also matter.

[RFC 6528](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6528), incorporated into RFC 9293, describes a clock component plus a keyed function of endpoint addresses/ports. RFC 9293 discusses an approximately 4 µs clock; actual implementations can differ. The construction aims to make new ISNs hard for an off-path attacker to predict while separating connection incarnations.

## Key takeaways

- The third handshake message acknowledges the server SYN and helps reject old connection attempts.
- Unpredictable ISNs resist off-path guessing, while connection-incarnation rules also guard against stale segments.
- Bidirectional reachability and cryptographic peer identity are different properties.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)
- [RFC 6528: Defending against Sequence Number Attacks](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6528)

questions.prompt: Why does a successful ordinary TCP three-way handshake fail to prove the cryptographic identity of the server?

options.text: It confirms sequence-space exchange and reachability, without a cryptographic identity proof.
options.explanation: Correct. TCP synchronises and acknowledges sequence spaces; a separate authenticated protocol such as TLS supplies cryptographic server identity.

options.text: Random initial sequence numbers are server certificates.
options.explanation: An unpredictable initial sequence number resists guessing but is not a signed identity credential.

options.text: The final ACK verifies the server hostname.
options.explanation: The final ACK acknowledges sequence space; TCP does not authenticate a hostname.

options.text: Only a fourth handshake message would authenticate the server.
options.explanation: Adding an unauthenticated message does not create cryptographic identity verification.

questions.workedExample:
1. The client sends its SYN.
2. The server acknowledges it and sends its own SYN.
3. The client acknowledges that SYN.
4. Those messages exchange and confirm sequence-space state, not a certificate or cryptographic proof of server identity. An authenticated higher-level protocol is still required.

lessons.title: SYN floods and cookie trade-offs
lessons.summary: How a SYN flood exhausts half-open state, and what SYN cookies trade away to resist it.
lessons.body:
## SYN floods and SYN cookies

When a server receives a SYN, normal stateful Linux processing creates **request-socket** state associated with the listener and sends SYN+ACK. Exact memory use depends on kernel/configuration. It retransmits the SYN+ACK if no ACK comes back. The Linux documentation retrieved here specifies five SYN+ACK retries by default with a one-second initial timeout that doubles each time: waits of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds put the last retry at 31 seconds, and one more doubled wait means the attempt is abandoned after about 63 seconds. This is a documented default, not a universal timing guarantee. It shows why half-open state is costly: each spoofed SYN can hold an entry for about a minute.

A **SYN flood** attempts to exhaust connection-establishment resources with SYN traffic, often using spoofed addresses. The final ACKs never arrive, the SYN queue fills with half-open entries, and real clients' SYNs are dropped. The attacker needs no completed connections and can hide behind random sources.

## SYN cookies

A **SYN cookie** avoids retaining an ordinary per-attempt half-open entry: encode enough information in the server's sequence-number construction to validate a returning ACK and reconstruct connection state. Secret keys and other shared server state still exist, and processing consumes CPU and bandwidth.

A conceptual flow is:

```
SYN + endpoint tuple
        |
        v
secret + time + supported option state
        |
        v
cookie sequence number -> SYN+ACK
        |
client returns ACK acknowledging cookie
        |
validate freshness/authenticator
        |
create established-connection state
```

The exact encoding is implementation-dependent. The client's ACK acknowledges the cookie plus one (a SYN uses one sequence number), so the server subtracts one, wrapping round at the 32-bit limit, to recover the cookie and then applies its validation rules. An off-path attacker that cannot observe the SYN+ACK must guess a valid value; finite cookie authenticators do not make guessing mathematically impossible.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A stamped ticket instead of a reservation book
> A busy venue stops writing everyone who turns up into a reservation book. Instead the door staff hand each person a ticket stamped with a secret mark and the time, with their party size written on it, and keep nothing themselves. When someone comes back with a ticket, staff check the mark and the time, read the party size off the ticket and seat them.
>
> **How it maps:** The reservation book is the SYN queue of half-open entries. The stamped ticket is the cookie carried in the server's initial sequence number, including the little option state (such as the MSS) it can encode. Coming back with the ticket is the client's ACK, which the server validates with its secret and a freshness check before creating the connection.
>
> **Where it stops:** A ticket has room for only a little information, just as a cookie can encode only limited MSS and option state. A forger who guesses the mark could still get in, and an attacker can still waste the staff's time and the doorway's capacity even without a book to fill.

Costs:

- Limited cookie space constrains the amount of MSS/option state encoded; the set of supported MSS values depends on the implementation.
- Option support can be reduced; implementations may encode extra state in negotiated timestamp fields. Behaviour varies by version and client options.
- Without per-attempt timer state, there is no autonomous SYN+ACK retransmission timer for that attempt. A retransmitted client SYN can elicit another SYN+ACK.

Linux has its own cookie construction. Its documented default, `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1`, sends cookies **only when the SYN queue overflows**, when the kernel is built with SYN-cookie support; value 2 requests unconditional generation. Cookies do not remedy every overload or network-capacity problem. Large providers also filter floods upstream, before they reach servers.

## Key takeaways

- Spoofed SYN traffic can consume state, processing and network resources before connections complete.
- SYN cookies validate a returning ACK without retaining an ordinary per-attempt half-open entry.
- Finite option/authenticator space, implementation choices and absent per-attempt timers constrain cookies.

## Further reading

- [RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4987)
- [SYN cookies — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SYN_cookies)
- [SYN packet handling in the wild — Cloudflare blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/syn-packet-handling-in-the-wild/)
- [Linux TCP configuration defaults](https://kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/ip-sysctl.html)

questions.prompt: On a Linux kernel built with SYN-cookie support and tcp_syncookies = 1, an overflowing SYN backlog triggers cookie mode for a new attempt. What is the main mechanism?

options.text: It doubles the SYN queue each time it fills, until memory runs out
options.explanation: Cookie mode avoids retaining the normal per-attempt half-open entry. It still uses shared secrets, processing time and network capacity.

options.text: It drops all SYNs from IP addresses it hasn't seen before
options.explanation: That is not the cookie mechanism. Source filtering may help separately, depending on reliable information and deployment.

options.text: It requires the client to solve a proof-of-work puzzle in the SYN
options.explanation: TCP has no such mechanism, and unmodified clients must keep working. SYN cookies need no client changes at all.

options.text: It omits the normal half-open entry, encodes reconstructable state in the sequence-number construction, and validates the returning ACK before creating the connection
options.explanation: Correct. The ACK acknowledges the cookie sequence number. Validation uses secret-dependent information and freshness checks; it reduces state-exhaustion risk without eliminating CPU/bandwidth costs or every possible guess.

questions.workedExample:
1. Normal stateful processing would keep a half-open entry for this attempt.
2. In overflow-triggered cookie mode, the server instead sends a checkable sequence number (the cookie) in its SYN+ACK and keeps no ordinary entry.
3. A genuine client acknowledges that number plus one, wrapping round to 0 past the largest 32-bit value, exactly as it would for any SYN+ACK.
4. The server subtracts one, validates the result with its secret and freshness checks, and reconstructs the supported state before creating the connection.
5. An off-path spoofer that never saw the SYN+ACK has to guess; a finite check value is not impossible to guess, and CPU and bandwidth can still be exhausted.

link.title: RFC 4987: TCP SYN flooding and mitigations

questions.prompt: For a SYN-cookie implementation that stores no ordinary per-attempt half-open entry and encodes MSS/limited option state in finite cookie space, which trade-offs can arise? Select all that apply.

options.text: MSS may need to be represented by one of a limited set of supported values
options.explanation: Correct for the stated design. The size and contents of that set are implementation-dependent; a universal eight-value table is not assumed.

options.text: Option negotiation can be restricted unless additional recoverable state is encoded, for example using timestamp fields
options.explanation: Correct. Support depends on the cookie construction, kernel version and client options; finite sequence-number space constrains the information available.

options.text: There is no autonomous per-attempt SYN+ACK retransmission timer without the corresponding state
options.explanation: Correct. A client retransmitting its SYN can still receive another SYN+ACK; “no retransmission timer” does not mean the server can never respond again.

options.text: Clients need a SYN-cookie-aware TCP stack to connect
options.explanation: SYN cookies are invisible to the client: it simply sees an ordinary ISN and echoes it plus one. That is why they were deployable.

options.text: On Linux, every connection uses cookies once they are enabled, even when the server is idle
options.explanation: Linux’s documented value 1 uses cookies on backlog overflow; value 2 enables unconditional generation when supported. Enabling the feature does not invariably mean all attempts use it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Limited encoded state can constrain MSS and option support.
2. Shared secrets remain, but this design does not retain a normal half-open entry with its own retransmission timer.
3. Repeated client SYNs may still trigger repeated replies.
4. Ordinary clients need no cookie-specific processing; they acknowledge the received sequence number.
5. Linux cookie-use policy depends on its configured mode. The first three options describe genuine trade-offs.

lessons.title: Graceful close, half-close and TIME_WAIT
lessons.summary: How each direction of a connection closes separately, and why the side that closes first waits in TIME_WAIT.
lessons.body:
## Closing: the four-way exchange

TCP connections are **full duplex**, so each direction is closed separately. Either side sends FIN to say "I have no more data". The other side acknowledges it, may keep sending, and later sends its own FIN.

```
A (active close)        B (passive)
ESTABLISHED             ESTABLISHED
  | FIN seq=8000          |
  |---------------------->| CLOSE_WAIT
FIN_WAIT_1                |
  |          ACK ack=8001 |
  |<----------------------|
FIN_WAIT_2                |
  |   (B may send more)   |
  |          FIN seq=9000 |
  |<----------------------| LAST_ACK
TIME_WAIT                 |
  | ACK ack=9001          |
  |---------------------->| CLOSED
(wait 2 x MSL)
CLOSED
```

B often combines its ACK and FIN into one segment, giving three segments in total. A **half-close** (`shutdown(SHUT_WR)` on A) sends a FIN but keeps receiving; that is how a client can say "that's my whole request" and still read the response.

## TIME_WAIT and 2×MSL

In the ordinary sequential graceful close above, the active closer ends in **TIME_WAIT**, and stays there for twice the **maximum segment lifetime** (MSL), the longest a segment is assumed to survive in the network. RFC 793 suggested an MSL of two minutes, which makes TIME_WAIT four minutes; real stacks often use a shorter fixed value.

Simultaneous close can put both endpoints in TIME_WAIT; aborts and special reuse cases follow different rules. Two purposes of TIME_WAIT are:

1. **A retransmitted FIN may need another ACK.** Keeping connection state lets the endpoint acknowledge a repeated FIN if the peer missed the final ACK. The TIME_WAIT timer can restart when the FIN is received again. MSL is a segment-lifetime assumption, not the peer's retransmission timeout, so adding two presumed network delays is not a proof of the retransmission schedule.
2. **Old duplicates must expire.** Retaining the connection incarnation for the specified interval reduces confusion if the same endpoint tuple is reused. The guarantee relies on the MSL/sequence-number assumptions; TCP also specifies constrained early-reuse cases.

Linux v6.12 defines its ordinary TIME_WAIT interval as **60 seconds**; reuse, retransmitted segments and resource handling can affect an observed entry’s lifetime.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Staying on the line after goodbye
> At the end of a phone call you say "Bye", they say "Bye", and you say "Bye then" one last time. You stay on the line a moment in case they did not hear your last word and say "Hello?" again, so you can answer.
>
> **How it maps:** The two goodbyes are the two FINs; your final "Bye then" is the last ACK. Lingering on the line is TIME_WAIT: the side that said goodbye first keeps the connection's state so it can acknowledge a repeated FIN, and so that stray old segments are not mistaken for a new call on the same tuple.
>
> **Where it stops:** On a phone you linger for a second; TCP waits a set interval (60 seconds on Linux) even when nothing arrives, and a repeated FIN can restart it. And a phone line carries no delayed words from an earlier call, whereas old TCP segments really can turn up late.

## Key takeaways

- TCP closes its two sending directions independently; half-close preserves the receiving direction.
- In an ordinary sequential close, the active closer enters TIME_WAIT.
- TIME_WAIT supports repeated-FIN acknowledgement and separation from old duplicates; implementation intervals differ from the historical MSL example.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)
- [Coping with the TCP TIME-WAIT state on busy Linux servers — Vincent Bernat](https://vincent.bernat.ch/en/blog/2014-tcp-time-wait-state-linux)

questions.prompt: A web server sends a FIN after its response. The browser receives and acknowledges that FIN before sending its own. Assume a successful sequential graceful close, no resets and no unread-data abort. Which endpoint enters TIME_WAIT?

options.text: The browser, because it sent the last FIN
options.explanation: The browser is the passive closer here. It goes CLOSE_WAIT, then LAST_ACK, then CLOSED when its FIN is acknowledged.

options.text: Both sides, for twice the MSL each
options.explanation: Both can enter TIME_WAIT on a simultaneous close. The question instead specifies a sequential close with the server active first.

options.text: Neither; TIME_WAIT only happens after an RST
options.explanation: TIME_WAIT belongs to normal graceful closure; an accepted abort normally discards connection state without that FIN-close sequence.

options.text: The server, because it sent the first FIN
options.explanation: Correct. The active closer (whoever sends the first FIN) goes FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, then TIME_WAIT after acknowledging the peer's FIN.

questions.workedExample:
1. The server calls `close()` and sends FIN. It is the **active closer**: ESTABLISHED to FIN_WAIT_1.
2. The browser ACKs (server moves to FIN_WAIT_2) and enters CLOSE_WAIT.
3. The browser closes and sends its FIN (LAST_ACK).
4. The server ACKs that FIN and enters **TIME_WAIT** for twice the maximum segment lifetime (MSL); Linux uses a fixed 60 s.
5. The browser receives the ACK and goes straight to CLOSED.

In this specified sequential close, the server enters TIME_WAIT. A simultaneous close can put both peers there.
