lessons.title: BBRv1 bandwidth and RTT estimation
lessons.summary: How BBR estimates bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT and paces packets from that model.
lessons.body:
## BBR: model the path

Google's **BBR** (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time, 2016) takes a different approach: it estimates path properties from delivery feedback and controls pacing/in-flight data from a model. The numerical details below describe **BBRv1 as implemented in Linux v6.12**, not all BBR versions.

- **BtlBw**: the bottleneck bandwidth, estimated using a windowed maximum of delivery-rate samples over ten packet-timed rounds in this version, with safeguards for limited sending and other conditions.
- **RTprop**: the round-trip propagation delay, estimated using a ten-second windowed minimum in this version. The estimate includes endpoint/serialization effects and may include persistent queueing; it is not pure physical propagation delay.

Their product is the BDP. BBR **paces** packets at about BtlBw and caps in-flight data at a small multiple of the BDP (a base gain near 2× in BBRv1, with minimum-window adjustments, allowances for ACKs that arrive in bunches, and others):

```formula reference
BDP = BtlBw RTprop
R_pace = g_p BtlBw
W_cap = g_c BDP
where
BDP: bandwidth-delay product, the data in flight that exactly fills the path, in bytes (B)
BtlBw: the estimated bottleneck bandwidth, in bytes per second (B/s)
RTprop: the estimated round-trip propagation time, in seconds (s)
R_pace: the pacing rate, how fast BBR releases packets, in bytes per second
g_p: the pacing gain for the current phase, for example 1.25, 1 or 0.75 in ProbeBW
W_cap: the cap on data in flight, in bytes
g_c: the congestion-window gain, about 2 in BBRv1
B/s: bytes per second
s: seconds
In words: BBR multiplies its bandwidth estimate by its minimum-RTT estimate to get the path's capacity in flight, sends at about its bandwidth estimate (nudged up or down by a phase gain), and allows roughly twice that capacity in flight.
```

For example, on a 100 Mbit/s bottleneck with a 20 ms base RTT, BBR aims to keep about 250 KB in the pipe and allows roughly twice that in flight. The ideal operating point is to keep the pipe full without building a queue.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A café manager pacing orders to the coffee machine
> Instead of taking every order and letting a queue form until people give up, a café manager watches two things: the most drinks per minute the machine has managed recently, and the shortest time a drink has recently taken from order to hand-over. The manager lets orders in at about the machine's pace, keeps just enough in progress to keep it busy, and now and then lets in a few extra to check whether the machine has got faster.
>
> **How it maps:** Drinks per minute is BtlBw; the shortest wait is RTprop; orders in progress is data in flight, capped near their product (the BDP); letting orders in at a steady pace is pacing; the occasional extra orders and the occasional pause are the ProbeBW and ProbeRTT phases.
>
> **Where it stops:** The manager can see the machine, but BBR infers both numbers from ACK timing, and other senders sharing the bottleneck can make its estimates wrong. BBR also still has to recover lost packets, which a café never has to do with a drink.

To observe available delivery capacity the sender must offer enough data; probing beyond it can build a queue and obscure the baseline RTT. Reducing in-flight data can help refresh the RTT estimate. These are estimation challenges, not a theorem that full utilisation always requires a queue. So BBR cycles through phases:

| Phase | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Startup | Pacing gain about 2.89, designed for rapid growth; exits after three qualifying rounds without 25% bandwidth growth |
| Drain | Gain below 1 to empty the queue Startup built |
| ProbeBW | Gains 1.25, 0.75, then six 1.0 phases; transitions use timing/in-flight checks |
| ProbeRTT | On qualifying minimum-RTT expiry, reduce toward 4 packets; duration includes at least 200 ms and a completed round |

BBRv1 aims to keep utilisation high without persistently filling queues and can avoid repeated Reno/CUBIC-style reductions for non-congestion loss. It still performs loss recovery and includes loss-related recovery/policer handling; “ignores all loss” is false. Results depend on the path and competing traffic, so there is no guaranteed speedup or fairness outcome.

Later BBR versions change the model and loss response. The **July 2026 BBRv3 IETF draft** retrieved here remains experimental and explicitly does **not** specify a particular ECN algorithm; if a connection advertises ECN support, however, CE marks must still be treated as congestion. Thus, claims that every BBRv2/v3 implementation has one common ECN algorithm are omitted. Linux BBR uses packet pacing, via `fq` or internal pacing support in the examined implementation.

## Key takeaways

- Linux v6.12 BBRv1 estimates recent delivery capacity and minimum RTT to control pacing and in-flight limits.
- Startup, Drain, ProbeBW and ProbeRTT serve different estimation and queue-management purposes.
- BBR versions differ; neither loss handling, ECN behaviour nor fairness is universal across all versions.

## Further reading

- [BBR: Congestion-Based Congestion Control — Google Research](https://research.google/pubs/bbr-congestion-based-congestion-control-2/)
- [Linux v6.12 BBRv1 implementation](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/net/ipv4/tcp_bbr.c)
- [BBRv3 IETF draft, July 2026](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-ccwg-bbr-06)

questions.prompt: In a controlled test with spare path capacity and random link loss, a service observes higher sustained throughput after switching the sender from CUBIC to BBRv1 while keeping loss detection and retransmission machinery unchanged. Which mechanism can explain this observation?

options.text: BBR uses a larger initial window
options.explanation: The initial window affects only the first few RTTs of a transfer. The difference here persists for the whole download.

options.text: BBR retransmits lost packets faster than CUBIC
options.explanation: Loss detection and retransmission (SACK, RACK) are shared machinery. The difference is how the sending rate reacts to loss.

options.text: BBRv1 bases its pacing model on measured delivery rate and minimum RTT rather than applying CUBIC’s multiplicative response to congestion events
options.explanation: Correct. This can make BBRv1 less sensitive to some random-loss patterns. It does not mean loss has no effect on its recovery, delivery-rate estimates or throughput.

options.text: BBR disables congestion control on lossy links
options.explanation: BBR still controls its rate, via pacing at its bandwidth estimate and capping in-flight data near the BDP. It just doesn't use loss as its main signal.

questions.workedExample: CUBIC reduces its window on congestion events, which can include random link losses misinterpreted as congestion. BBRv1 instead uses a delivery-rate/minimum-RTT model, with additional recovery and policing behaviour. That difference can explain the measured improvement; it does not guarantee one on every path. A 1% packet-loss rate does not imply only a 1% throughput penalty, and the Reno-oriented Mathis approximation is not a general CUBIC formula.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe BBRv1 in Linux v6.12? Select all that apply.

options.text: It tracks a minimum-RTT estimate over a nominal 10-second window
options.explanation: Correct. This is an estimate of low-queue RTT, not a guaranteed measurement of pure propagation delay.

options.text: On expiry of its minimum-RTT estimate, eligible ProbeRTT operation reduces its cwnd target to four packets
options.explanation: Correct. After in-flight data falls sufficiently, completion requires the 200 ms interval and a packet-timed round. Idle restart and other state conditions matter; this is not an unconditional ten-second schedule.

options.text: In ProbeBW it cycles its pacing gain, briefly sending at 1.25× its bandwidth estimate and then 0.75×
options.explanation: Correct. The gain cycle contains 1.25, 0.75 and six 1.0 gains, with conditions controlling phase advancement.

options.text: It halves its sending rate on every packet loss, like Reno
options.explanation: BBRv1 does not use loss as its primary congestion signal; that is its defining difference. (Later versions add bounded loss responses.)

options.text: It requires the receiver to run BBR too
options.explanation: The receiver does not need to run BBR as its own sending algorithm. This is sender-side TCP congestion control.

questions.workedExample: Linux v6.12 BBRv1 uses a ten-packet-round maximum delivery-rate filter and a nominal ten-second minimum-RTT window. ProbeBW has gains 1.25, 0.75, then six 1.0 phases. Eligible ProbeRTT operation targets four packets and requires its timing/round conditions. It neither halves its sending rate on every packet loss nor requires a BBR receiver. These details should not be silently generalised to later BBR versions.

lessons.title: ECN marks, DCTCP and sender selection
lessons.summary: How ECN signals congestion by marking packets instead of dropping them, and how DCTCP scales its response.
lessons.body:
## ECN: congestion without loss

Loss-oriented algorithms can also react to explicit congestion indications. **Explicit Congestion Notification** ([RFC 3168](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3168)) lets a router **mark** a packet instead of dropping it:

1. In classic TCP ECN (RFC 3168), both sides negotiate ECN capability in the handshake. Later ECN schemes have different feedback details.
2. Packets are sent with an ECN-capable codepoint in the IP header.
3. A capable queue-management algorithm may set **CE** (Congestion Experienced) on eligible packets instead of dropping; overload and policy can still cause drops.
4. The receiver echoes it with **ECE** in its ACKs; the sender reduces cwnd as for a loss and replies with **CWR**.

A delivered CE-marked packet does not need retransmission merely because it was marked. ECN does not prevent unrelated loss or guarantee a one-RTT improvement. Data-centre algorithms such as **DCTCP** ([RFC 8257](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8257)) go further, scaling the reduction by the **fraction** of marked packets to keep queues tiny:

```formula reference
α_new = (1 − g)α + gM
cwnd_new = cwnd(1 − α_new / 2)
where
α: alpha, DCTCP's running estimate of the fraction of data that is being marked, from 0 to 1
α_new: the updated estimate after one window of data
g: the weight given to the newest measurement, between 0 and 1; RFC 8257 notes that 1/16 is used in some implementations
M: the fraction of bytes acknowledged in the last window of data that carried a CE mark
cwnd: the congestion window before the reduction
cwnd_new: the window after the reduction
In words: DCTCP keeps a running average of the fraction of its data that was marked; if almost nothing is marked it cuts the window only a little, and if everything is marked it halves the window like Reno.
```

So DCTCP's response is graded: a queue that exceeds the switch's marking threshold only briefly produces few marks and a small trim rather than a halving, which lets data-centre switches keep their queues short.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A "kitchen busy" sticker instead of a thrown-away order
> A busy kitchen could cope with overload by throwing some orders away, and the waiter would learn of the problem only when a customer complained. Instead, the kitchen puts a "kitchen busy" sticker on plates it still serves, and the waiter, seeing the stickers, takes orders more slowly.
>
> **How it maps:** Throwing orders away is a router dropping packets; the sticker is the CE mark on a packet that is still delivered; the waiter noticing it is the receiver echoing ECE to the sender, which reduces its congestion window. DCTCP is a waiter who slows down in proportion to how many plates carry stickers.
>
> **Where it stops:** The waiter sees the sticker straight away, whereas the mark reaches the sender only through the receiver's ACKs, about a round trip later. And marking works only when both endpoints negotiate ECN, the congested router supports it and devices along the path leave the ECN bits intact; otherwise the router copes by dropping.

## Choosing and checking

Example Linux inspection commands (shown output is illustrative, not a guaranteed default):

```
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = cubic
$ ss -ti   # per-connection cwnd, rtt
```

An application can choose per socket with the `TCP_CONGESTION` option. Congestion control runs on the **sender**, so a server can change its TCP sender algorithm without requiring the client to use the same algorithm. Whether performance improves must be measured; receiver feedback and available implementation support still matter.

## Key takeaways

- Classic ECN negotiates capability and echoes delivered CE marks using TCP flags.
- A mark signals congestion without making the marked packet itself require retransmission.
- DCTCP scales a reduction using a smoothed marked-data fraction; sender algorithm selection remains implementation-dependent.

## Further reading

- [RFC 3168: Explicit Congestion Notification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3168)
- [TCP congestion control — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCP_congestion_control)

questions.prompt: Two hosts negotiate classic RFC 3168 ECN. A router marks one ECN-capable data packet CE and the packet arrives. Assume a new congestion event, successful feedback and no packet loss. What happens next?

options.text: The receiver discards the marked packet and the sender retransmits it
options.explanation: The marked packet is delivered normally. ECN's whole point is signalling congestion without losing data.

options.text: The receiver echoes congestion with ECE; the sender reduces its congestion window and signals CWR, without retransmitting solely because of the mark
options.explanation: Correct. Classic ECN feeds congestion information back without requiring the marked packet to be lost. No fixed latency advantage over every loss-detection method is implied.

options.text: The router sends an ICMP message to the sender asking it to slow down
options.explanation: That resembles the long-deprecated ICMP Source Quench. ECN signals in-band, via IP and TCP header bits.

options.text: Nothing; ECN marks are only used for statistics
options.explanation: The sender must respond to ECE by reducing its window, or ECN would provide no congestion control.

questions.workedExample:
1. The router forwards the CE-marked packet.
2. The receiver echoes congestion using ECE until CWR acknowledges the response.
3. For the specified new congestion event, the sender performs its congestion response and signals CWR. Repeated ECE ACKs do not require a fresh reduction for every ACK.
4. The delivered mark alone requires no retransmission. ECN does not prevent other packets being lost or guarantee freedom from timeouts.

lessons.title: Counting setup and response round trips
lessons.summary: Why small transfers are limited by round trips rather than bandwidth, and what saves those round trips.
lessons.body:
The previous lessons explained how TCP works. This one asks why a transfer is slower than the link, and what engineers at CDNs, browser vendors and cloud providers do about it.

There are three usual suspects:

1. **Round trips**: handshakes and slow start, which bound short transfers.
2. **Loss**: which bounds long transfers through congestion control.
3. **Queues**: which add delay that nobody asked for.

Deployment is another constraint: transport changes must work with deployed endpoints and middleboxes. QUIC provides an alternative design over UDP.

## Short transfers are latency-bound

For small responses on a sufficiently fast link, handshake and request round trips can dominate. Serialization, server work, DNS, certificate size and loss can also matter.

Illustrative model: fetch 100,000 payload bytes over a new TCP + TLS 1.3 connection at 100 ms RTT, with MSS 1,460 bytes, initial window 10 segments, ideal doubling per completed flight, negligible serialization/server processing, no DNS delay, no loss, no TLS retry and no other limits. Ignore handshake bytes when modelling the response window:

| Step | Round trips |
|---|---|
| TCP handshake | 1 |
| TLS 1.3 handshake | 1 |
| Request, then slow start: 10, 20, 39 segments | 3 |
| Total | about 5 (500 ms) |

The response needs 69 segments, sent in flights of 10, 20 and 39. The request/first response costs one RTT; each further flight adds one RTT in this ideal model. Five round trips at 100 ms is about half a second, and only the last three carry the actual data. Note what does not appear: the link's bandwidth. On a fast link, a faster link would barely change this total; fewer round trips or shorter ones would.

A conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake adds a round trip relative to TLS 1.3; resumptions differ. The table is an estimate under these assumptions, not a measured or universal HTTPS latency. Connection reuse and closer servers can reduce round-trip costs.

> [!note] TCP Fast Open
> TFO ([RFC 7413](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7413)) can let a client with a previously obtained cookie send data in its SYN. When supported and accepted, this can save a round trip. Applications must handle replay-related restrictions and implementations need fallback for incompatible paths. This lesson makes no current browser-adoption claim.

## Key takeaways

- Setup and slow-start response flights can dominate a short transfer on a fast path.
- The five-RTT worked example makes all handshake, flight and processing assumptions explicit.
- Reuse and eligible Fast Open can reduce setup costs without guaranteeing a universal latency.

## Further reading

- [RFC 7413: TCP Fast Open](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7413)
- [RFC 9000: QUIC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)

questions.prompt: A mobile app's small API calls (about 10 KB each) take about 150 ms on a 50 ms RTT path. A trace shows every call opens a new TCP connection and a full TLS 1.3 handshake, and each response fits within the initial congestion window. Which change would cut the latency the most?

options.text: Upgrade the server's link from 1 Gbit/s to 10 Gbit/s
options.explanation: A 10 KB response takes well under a millisecond to serialise at either speed. The time is spent in round trips, not in transmission.

options.text: Reuse one open connection (HTTP keep-alive or connection pooling) for successive calls
options.explanation: Correct. With a usable open connection, a call needs only the request/response round trip: about 50 ms instead of about 150 ms.

options.text: Increase the client's receive window
options.explanation: The response already fits in the first flight; a bigger window cannot remove the two handshake round trips.

options.text: Switch the server's congestion control from CUBIC to BBR
options.explanation: With the response inside the initial window, congestion-control growth does not limit this exchange. The handshakes do.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count the round trips for a fresh call: one for the TCP handshake, one for TLS 1.3, and one for the request and its response, since 10 KB fits in a 10-segment initial window. Three round trips of 50 ms is about 150 ms, which matches the measurement.
2. Bandwidth barely matters: 10 KB is tiny compared with what the link moves in a round trip.
3. A bigger receive window or a different congestion-control algorithm does not remove any round trips for a response that already fits in the first flight.
4. Reusing an open connection removes both handshake round trips, leaving about 50 ms per call. TLS resumption with early data, TCP Fast Open or QUIC can cut setup on new connections, with their own conditions.

lessons.title: The Mathis model and its limits
lessons.summary: The Mathis model: why a Reno-style flow's throughput falls with RTT and with the square root of the loss rate.
lessons.body:
## Long transfers are loss-bound: the Mathis formula

The Mathis model approximates a sustained Reno-style congestion-avoidance flow with light/moderate loss, sufficient sender data and receive window, and no retransmission timeouts. It answers a practical question: how much throughput can a given loss rate allow on a given path? The ideal periodic-loss sawtooth, with one ACK per segment, yields:

```formula essential
X ≈ (MSS / RTT) × (C / √p)
where
X: the estimated throughput, in bytes per second (multiply by 8 for bits per second)
MSS: maximum segment size, the payload bytes per segment, for example 1,460 bytes
RTT: round-trip time, in seconds
C: a constant from the sawtooth shape, about 1.22 (the square root of 3/2) for one ACK per segment and periodic loss
p: the loss rate: the fraction of packets lost, for example 0.0001 for one in ten thousand
√: square root: the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value inside; √0.0001 = 0.01
≈: approximately equal to
In words: throughput is about one segment per round trip, scaled up by 1.22 divided by the square root of the loss rate.
```

Where does the square root come from? The sawtooth. With one loss in every 1/p packets, the window climbs from half its peak back to its peak at one segment per round trip. Both the number of round trips in a cycle and the average window are proportional to the peak, so the packets sent per cycle grow with the **square** of the peak. Rarer losses therefore let the window climb higher, but only with one over the square root of the loss rate. The [Mathis et al. paper](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lam/395t/papers/Mathis1998.pdf) gives the full derivation.

For a sense of scale, with 1,460-byte segments and a 100 ms RTT the formula returns about **14 Mbit/s** at a 0.01% loss rate and about **1.4 Mbit/s** at 1%. These are model outputs, not universal caps or predictions for arbitrary packet-loss patterns. ACK behaviour and loss patterns change the constant; timeouts and other limits can invalidate the approximation. Notice that the link's capacity does not appear at all. Within the model:

- **Throughput is inversely proportional to RTT.** Doubling RTT halves the estimate when all other parameters stay fixed. Geographic distance does not by itself determine RTT.
- **Throughput falls with the square root of loss.** To double throughput you need **four times** less loss; quadrupling the loss rate halves it.
- **Long fat pipes need tiny loss rates**, which is why CUBIC and BBR exist. This Reno model is not a general throughput law for CUBIC or BBR.

Use the formula as a teaching comparison, not a unique diagnosis. Matching it does not rule out other bottlenecks. `ss -ti` exposes TCP state and counters on Linux; its retransmission counters are not automatically the model’s loss probability. Compare captures, application demand, receive windows, congestion-control state and link utilisation.

## Key takeaways

- The Mathis approximation describes a qualified Reno-style loss/RTT model without retransmission timeouts.
- Its square-root dependence follows from the ideal sawtooth packet count.
- The formula is a comparison tool rather than a universal TCP ceiling or a unique bottleneck diagnosis.

## Further reading

- [The Macroscopic Behavior of the TCP Congestion Avoidance Algorithm — Mathis et al.](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lam/395t/papers/Mathis1998.pdf)
- [Mathis and Mahdavi: Deprecating the TCP Macroscopic Model (2019 editorial)](https://ccronline.sigcomm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/acmdl19-323.pdf)

questions.prompt:
A Reno-style bulk transfer between two data centres 100 ms apart sees a steady 0.01% packet loss and runs at about 14 Mbit/s on a 1 Gbit/s link. The Mathis model fits its behaviour:

```formula
X ≈ (MSS / RTT) × (C / √p)
where
X: estimated throughput
MSS: payload bytes per segment, 1,460 here
RTT: round-trip time, 100 ms here
C: the model constant, about 1.22
p: the loss rate, 0.0001 here
√: square root
≈: approximately equal to
In words: throughput is about one segment per round trip, times 1.22 over the square root of the loss rate.
```

An engineer proposes upgrading the link to 10 Gbit/s. What does the model predict?

options.text: About ten times the throughput, roughly 140 Mbit/s
options.explanation: Link capacity does not appear in the model. The flow is limited by its loss rate and round trip, not by the link, which is already mostly idle.

options.text: Little or no improvement; reducing the loss rate or the RTT, or using a congestion-control algorithm less sensitive to random loss, would help instead
options.explanation: Correct. In the model, throughput depends on segment size, RTT and loss rate. Quartering the loss would double it; halving the RTT would also double it; a faster link would not.

options.text: Throughput falls, because a faster link drops more packets
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario says the loss rate rises with the upgrade. Under the stated model the link speed simply does not enter.

options.text: About 1.22 times the throughput, because of the model constant
options.explanation: The constant comes from the sawtooth shape; it does not scale with link speed.

questions.workedExample:
1. The formula contains segment size, round-trip time and loss rate. Link capacity is absent.
2. At 14 Mbit/s the flow uses under 2% of the 1 Gbit/s link, so capacity is clearly not the limit; a faster link changes none of the model's inputs.
3. What would help: lowering the loss rate (a quarter of the loss doubles the throughput, because of the square root), lowering the RTT (half the RTT doubles it), larger segments, or several parallel flows.
4. In practice, switching to an algorithm that reacts less to random loss, such as BBR, can also help; the Mathis model describes Reno-style behaviour only.
5. Check first that the model fits: retransmission counters are not automatically the model's loss probability, and other bottlenecks can coexist.

questions.prompt: A Reno-style flow that fits the Mathis model is moved to a path with **four times** the RTT and **four times** the loss rate. By roughly what factor does the model's throughput estimate change?

options.text: It falls to about a sixteenth
options.explanation: This divides by 4 for the loss as well as 4 for the RTT. The loss rate enters only through its square root, so four times the loss costs a factor of 2.

options.text: It falls to about an eighth
options.explanation: Correct. Four times the RTT divides the estimate by four; four times the loss divides it by the square root of four, which is two. Together that is an eighth.

options.text: It falls to about a quarter
options.explanation: This accounts for the RTT but forgets the higher loss rate.

options.text: It falls to about a half
options.explanation: This accounts for the loss but forgets that throughput is inversely proportional to RTT.

questions.workedExample:
1. In the model, throughput is inversely proportional to the RTT: four times the RTT gives a quarter of the throughput.
2. Throughput is inversely proportional to the **square root** of the loss rate: four times the loss gives half the throughput.
3. The factors multiply: a quarter of a half is an eighth.
4. So a flow that managed 71 Mbit/s would drop to about 9 Mbit/s. Distance, loss and RTT compound; closer servers and cleaner paths both help, but geography alone does not determine RTT or measured throughput.

lessons.title: Queueing delay, bufferbloat and AQM
lessons.summary: How oversized queues add latency without adding throughput, and how CoDel and fq_codel fight back.
lessons.body:
## Bufferbloat

Routers need buffers to absorb bursts. The traditional rule of thumb was one BDP of buffering per link. But memory became cheap, and many home routers, cable modems and mobile base stations were built with **far** more.

A saturated loss-based flow with a large tail-drop queue can sustain substantial queue occupancy: Reno and CUBIC keep growing their windows until the buffer is full and packets are dropped. ECN, AQM, competing traffic and sender limits change this behaviour. For a packet joining a FIFO, the wait is the backlog ahead of it divided by the rate at which the link drains it.

```formula reference
T_q = Q / R
where
T_q: queueing delay, how long a newly arrived packet waits before its own transmission starts, in seconds (s)
Q: the backlog queued ahead of it, in bits (multiply bytes by 8)
R: the rate at which the link drains the queue, in bits per second (bit/s)
s: seconds
bit/s: bits per second
In words: the wait is the amount queued ahead divided by how fast the link sends it, so a bigger full buffer or a slower link means a longer wait.
```

For example, 256 KiB queued at a 2 Mbit/s uplink is about 2.1 million bits, so a packet joining the back waits about a second, ignoring overhead and changes in link rate. Other queues or priority classes can see different delays. Sustained excessive queueing is **bufferbloat**: high throughput can coexist with poor latency under load. Every packet that waits behind that backlog, including a video call's or a game's, has about a second added to its round trip: a 20 ms idle path becomes a path of over a second while the upload runs.

Note what the bigger buffer did *not* do: the upload's throughput is set by the uplink rate, which is already fully used. Extra buffering beyond what bursts need only adds waiting.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A longer queue at the same single till
> A shop with one till installs a much longer waiting lane. The cashier serves customers no faster, so the shop takes the same money per hour, but each customer now waits far longer, including someone who only wants to buy a stamp.
>
> **How it maps:** The cashier's speed is the link rate; the waiting lane is the router buffer; the customers are packets. A bigger buffer, kept full by a loss-based sender, adds waiting time without adding throughput, and the person with a stamp is the latency-sensitive flow stuck behind the bulk upload.
>
> **Where it stops:** People in a queue leave when it gets too long, whereas a TCP sender keeps the queue topped up until packets are dropped or marked. And AQM has no shop equivalent: it deliberately drops or marks packets early to tell senders to slow down.

## Active queue management

Active queue management signals congestion before excessive persistent queues develop. Delay is the signal used by CoDel; other AQM designs use other measurements:

- **CoDel** (Controlled Delay, [RFC 8289](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8289)) tracks how long packets wait. Its usual target and interval are 5 ms and 100 ms. Persistent excess sojourn time can trigger drops or ECN marks; a remaining-backlog check avoids needlessly starving the link. The target is not a guaranteed maximum for every packet’s delay, and finite buffers can still drop bursts.
- **fq_codel** ([RFC 8290](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8290)) adds **flow queueing**: packets are hashed into queues, with modified deficit round-robin scheduling and CoDel. This reduces interference between bulk and sparse traffic; hash collisions and shared bottlenecks mean isolation is not absolute.
- **L4S** ([RFC 9330](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9330)) describes an architecture using scalable congestion control and compatible ECN/AQM behaviour to target low queueing delay. It is not merely a replacement name for CoDel or a guarantee of one-millisecond end-to-end latency.

**Pacing** spreads transmissions and can reduce bursts; **BBR** uses a path model but can still build queues. Locate the actual bottleneck. When it is an inaccessible modem/ISP queue, suitable shaping on a controlled router can move the bottleneck to a queue where AQM is effective; measure the throughput trade-off.

## Key takeaways

- FIFO backlog divided by service rate estimates waiting time before transmission under fixed-rate assumptions.
- Persistent excess queueing can coexist with high throughput and harm latency.
- CoDel, flow queueing, pacing and shaping address related but distinct causes of delay.

## Further reading

- [Introduction to bufferbloat — bufferbloat.net](https://www.bufferbloat.net/projects/bloat/wiki/Introduction/)
- [RFC 8289: Controlled Delay Active Queue Management](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8289)

questions.prompt: Whenever someone in a house uploads a large video, everyone's video calls stutter and web pages load slowly, even though download bandwidth is plentiful. Ping times jump from 20 ms to over a second. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The upload is using UDP, which has no congestion control
options.explanation: UDP itself has no congestion-control algorithm, but protocols running over it can provide one. The observed delay does not identify the transport protocol.

options.text: The ISP is throttling the household
options.explanation: A rate limit can contribute to queueing, depending on its implementation. The leading explanation for this load-correlated delay is an excessive standing queue; confirm it by measurement.

options.text: Bufferbloat: a persistent queue at a shared uplink delays other traffic using that queue
options.explanation: Correct as the leading hypothesis. For a FIFO packet, delay is approximately the queued work ahead divided by service rate; not every packet or priority class necessarily sees the same backlog.

options.text: TCP's receive window on the video-call server is too small
options.explanation: A small receive window can limit that connection’s sending allowance, but it does not by itself explain the observed load-correlated ping delay. A shared uplink queue is the leading hypothesis; queue classes and traffic paths determine which packets are affected.

questions.workedExample:
1. A large increase in RTT that appears only while the upload runs is the signature of a standing queue at a shared bottleneck, usually the home uplink.
2. If traffic shares a FIFO, each packet waits for the backlog ahead of it to drain: about a quarter of a megabyte queued on a 2 Mbit/s uplink adds roughly a second.
3. The upload keeps that queue full because a loss-based sender grows its window until the buffer is full and drops packets, so every other packet through that queue inherits the delay.
4. Identify the bottleneck and queue discipline before concluding. AQM (such as fq_codel) and appropriate shaping at a controlled router can reduce queueing, with configuration and throughput trade-offs.

questions.prompt: An ISP doubles the buffer in a customer's cable modem, from about 250 KB to 500 KB, to reduce packet drops during large uploads. The uplink rate is unchanged, the modem holds everything in one first-in, first-out queue, and the uploads use a loss-based congestion control such as CUBIC with no AQM or ECN. What happens to a video call that shares the uplink while an upload runs?

options.text: Its latency improves, because fewer packets are dropped
options.explanation: Fewer drops on the bulk upload do not make the call's packets travel faster. They still wait behind everything queued ahead of them.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the uplink rate is the same
options.explanation: The rate is the same, but the queue in front of each packet is longer, so each packet waits longer.

options.text: Its queueing delay roughly doubles, because the upload fills the bigger buffer and the call's packets wait behind twice the backlog, with no gain in upload throughput
options.explanation: Correct. A loss-based sender keeps growing its window until the full buffer drops packets. Wait time is backlog divided by drain rate, so twice the backlog at the same rate is about twice the delay.

options.text: The upload becomes twice as fast, so it finishes sooner and the call is affected for less time
options.explanation: The upload is limited by the uplink rate, which is already fully used. A bigger buffer adds waiting, not capacity.

questions.workedExample:
1. A loss-based sender such as CUBIC keeps increasing its window until packets are dropped. With a tail-drop FIFO, that means it keeps the buffer close to full.
2. Doubling the buffer therefore roughly doubles the standing backlog during the upload.
3. A packet's wait is the backlog ahead of it divided by the drain rate. Same uplink rate, twice the backlog: about twice the queueing delay for every packet that shares the queue, including the video call's.
4. The upload gains nothing: the uplink was already sending as fast as it can. This is bufferbloat.
5. The fixes target the queue, not the buffer size alone: AQM such as CoDel or fq_codel, ECN, or shaping at a router you control.

questions.prompt: A previously idle CoDel queue uses target 5 ms and interval 100 ms. No hard buffer limit is reached. Case A spikes to 40 ms but empties within 20 ms. Case B remains at 30–40 ms for seconds with sufficient backlog to satisfy CoDel’s remaining-byte check. Which behaviour is expected?

options.text: It drops packets in both cases, because delay exceeded 5 ms
options.explanation: Exceeding the target briefly does not alone trigger CoDel’s persistent-delay response. A burst could still encounter a finite-buffer limit, which this question excludes.

options.text: It drops in case A only, because sudden spikes are the problem
options.explanation: Bursts are what buffers exist for. The harmful case is the standing queue in B, which adds delay without adding throughput.

options.text: It doesn't drop in either case; CoDel only drops when the buffer is full
options.explanation: CoDel can signal persistent queueing before the buffer fills. It also retains checks intended to avoid starving the link.

options.text: It leaves case A alone, and in case B starts dropping (or ECN-marking), at increasing frequency while the delay stays above target
options.explanation: Correct. In B, the minimum delay over every 100 ms interval stays above 5 ms, which signals a standing queue. Responsive senders can reduce their offered load; the response depends on the protocol, congestion-control algorithm and delivered feedback.

questions.workedExample:
1. CoDel watches how long packets wait (their sojourn time), and in particular the minimum over each 100 ms interval.
2. Case A spikes but empties within 20 ms, so the minimum delay over a full interval does not stay above the 5 ms target. That is a burst, which is exactly what buffers are for, and CoDel leaves it alone (barring a full buffer, which the question excludes).
3. Case B stays at 30–40 ms for seconds, with enough backlog: the minimum over every interval is above target. That is a standing queue, so CoDel enters its dropping (or ECN-marking) state.
4. While the delay stays above target, its control law shrinks the gap between signals in proportion to one over the square root of how many signals it has sent so far, so it signals more and more often until senders respond.
5. Actual delay still depends on how the traffic responds; 5 ms is a target, not a per-packet guarantee.

lessons.title: Stream delivery gaps and ossification
lessons.summary: Why one lost segment stalls every HTTP/2 stream on a TCP connection, and why TCP is hard to change.
lessons.body:
## Head-of-line blocking

TCP delivers one ordered byte stream. If one segment is lost, later stream bytes cannot be delivered in order until the gap is filled (or the connection fails), even if those bytes belong to an unrelated request.

That matters for **HTTP/2**, which multiplexes many streams over a single TCP connection:

```
TCP stream:  [css][js][img1][img2]
loss in js:        ^
css: delivered
later bytes wait for gap recovery
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: One checkout queue for several shoppers' items
> Several shoppers put their items on one conveyor belt at a single till, separated by dividers. If the cashier must re-check the price of one item, everything behind it on the belt waits, including the next shoppers' items, even though their purchases have nothing to do with it.
>
> **How it maps:** The belt is the single TCP byte stream; each shopper's items are an HTTP/2 stream; the price check is a lost segment being retransmitted. Because TCP must hand over bytes strictly in order, data for unrelated streams waits behind the gap.
>
> **Where it stops:** A cashier could set the problem item aside and carry on; TCP cannot, because it knows nothing about streams. QUIC behaves like separate belts sharing one cashier: a gap holds up only its own stream, although all streams still share congestion and flow control.

Multiple HTTP/1.1 connections have separate TCP delivery ordering; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on a connection. A TCP gap blocks later bytes on that connection, not resources already delivered or other connections. Recovery has no fixed one-RTT duration. Which HTTP version is faster depends on the workload, implementation and path.

## Ossification: why TCP is hard to change

TCP commonly runs in OS kernels, although user-space implementations exist. Devices along a path may inspect or rewrite it:

- **NATs and firewalls** track TCP state, rewrite ports and sometimes sequence numbers.
- **Middleboxes** strip unknown options, normalise headers, or drop packets that look unusual. Compatibility therefore needs testing and fallback. Multipath TCP includes fallback to ordinary TCP when its negotiation does not succeed.
- **Deployment dependencies** can include OS updates and peer support, depending on the extension. Sender-only congestion-control changes need not update both endpoints.

These constraints contribute to **ossification**: deployed equipment’s assumptions can restrict protocol evolution. This does not mean every TCP change takes a decade or that extensions have stopped.

## Key takeaways

- A missing TCP range holds up later bytes on that connection, including multiplexed HTTP/2 streams.
- Other connections and already delivered bytes do not acquire that same delivery dependency.
- Deployed middlebox assumptions can obstruct extensions, making negotiation and fallback important.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9000: QUIC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment — Google (SIGCOMM 2017)](https://research.google/pubs/the-quic-transport-protocol-design-and-internet-scale-deployment/)

questions.prompt: A page loads 20 resources over a single HTTP/2 connection on TCP. One segment carrying part of a JavaScript file is lost. What happens to the other 19 resources' data that arrives just after it?

options.text: It waits in the receiver's TCP buffer until the lost segment is retransmitted, because TCP delivers bytes strictly in order
options.explanation: Correct. TCP doesn't know about HTTP/2 streams; it only sees one byte stream, and it can't deliver later bytes past a hole. This is transport-level head-of-line blocking.

options.text: It is delivered immediately; only the JavaScript stream waits
options.explanation: QUIC removes the requirement for a stream to wait solely for another stream’s missing bytes. Shared flow control, congestion control and application dependencies can still delay delivery. TCP uses one ordered byte stream.

options.text: It is discarded and must be resent too
options.explanation: Out-of-order data can be retained and reported with SACK when negotiated. Receivers can also discard buffered data, so retention is not an unconditional guarantee.

options.text: The browser opens a new connection for the remaining resources
options.explanation: TCP handles this gap on the existing connection. The supplied scenario does not imply that the browser opens a replacement connection; doing so would require application-level recovery logic.

questions.workedExample: HTTP/2 frames share TCP byte ordering. Later bytes cannot be delivered past the missing range until it is recovered; data already delivered is unaffected. Recovery duration is not fixed at one RTT. QUIC removes this cross-stream byte-order dependency, but shared congestion control, flow control and application dependencies can still delay multiple streams.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms can make transport extensions harder to deploy or help QUIC evolve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Some middleboxes interfere with unfamiliar TCP options or SYN data
options.explanation: Correct. Compatibility and fallback matter; this is not a claim that every middlebox behaves this way.

options.text: A TCP change in a kernel stack can depend on OS deployment cycles; a QUIC library can be updated with an application
options.explanation: Correct. Some TCP changes are sender-only, and neither TCP nor QUIC is required to live exclusively in one implementation layer.

options.text: Protecting QUIC control frames and selected header fields reduces the information middleboxes can depend on
options.explanation: Correct. Some wire fields remain visible and Initial keys are publicly derivable, so encryption does not eliminate all ossification or interference.

options.text: The TCP header has no room for any options
options.explanation: The base TCP header allows up to 40 option bytes. That finite space can constrain extensions too, but it is not zero; unfamiliar-option handling by middleboxes is a separate deployment obstacle.

options.text: The IETF has forbidden new TCP extensions since QUIC was standardised
options.explanation: TCP is still being extended (for example RACK-TLP in 2021 and AccECN, RFC 9768, in 2026). Deployment, not permission, is the barrier.

questions.workedExample: The first three describe compatibility, implementation deployment and protection mechanisms. The base TCP header permits up to 40 option bytes, and TCP standards work continues. None of these mechanisms guarantees a fixed adoption speed.

lessons.title: QUIC streams, migration and deployment
lessons.summary: What QUIC changes compared with TCP plus TLS, what it costs, and a practical tuning checklist.
lessons.body:
## QUIC: the transport in user space

**QUIC** ([RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)), started at Google and standardised in 2021, is the transport under **HTTP/3**. It runs over UDP (the UDP and ports units) and can be implemented in application **libraries** without changing the kernel; the protocol does not mandate an implementation location. Its design answers each of the problems above.

| Problem | QUIC's answer |
|---|---|
| Handshake RTTs | Combined transport/TLS setup; eligible 0-RTT sends early data, with replay restrictions |
| Head-of-line blocking | Per-stream ordering avoids TCP’s connection-wide delivery gap; shared limits remain |
| Ossification | Protected QUIC frames reduce ossification; some fields remain observable |
| Slow deployment | Can ship in application libraries |
| Network changes | Connection IDs support eligible, validated client migration |

A few details worth knowing:

- **Protection.** QUIC protects payloads, including ACK and other QUIC frames, and masks selected header bits and packet numbers. Connection IDs and other fields remain observable. Initial packet keys are publicly derivable, so Initial protection does not provide confidentiality against an observer. The optional spin bit can assist RTT estimation.
- **Loss recovery.** A newly transmitted packet uses a new packet number within its packet-number space; stream data may be resent at the same stream offset. This removes TCP's original-versus-retransmission ACK ambiguity. It does not make loss detection infallible: reordering can still cause spurious loss declarations.
- **Migration.** After handshake confirmation, connection IDs can support client migration, subject to negotiated restrictions, address validation and a working new path. A zero-length connection ID constrains migration. Success and seamless latency are not guaranteed.
- **Shared effects.** Loss can reduce a connection's congestion window, and flow control or application dependencies can delay several streams. QUIC removes the requirement to wait for an unrelated stream's missing bytes; it does not promise complete independence.
- **Congestion control.** RFC 9002 gives a NewReno-like example; compatible alternatives can be implemented. A library deployment can update the algorithm without an OS upgrade.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A case reference number on a support call
> When a support call drops, you ring back from a different phone and quote your case reference; the agent picks up where you left off. If the company filed cases under the caller's phone number instead, a new phone would mean starting again.
>
> **How it maps:** TCP files a connection under its addresses and ports, so a phone moving from Wi-Fi to 5G gets a new address and the connection cannot follow. QUIC's connection ID is the case reference: the server finds the existing connection even though the packets come from a new address.
>
> **Where it stops:** QUIC does not simply trust the reference: it validates the new path before sending much data there, and endpoints use fresh connection IDs on a new path so observers cannot easily link the old and new addresses. Migration also needs the server to allow it and the new path to work.

## The costs of QUIC

- **CPU.** Encryption, packet processing, batching and offload support affect cost. Compare QUIC with the actual alternative, often TCP **plus TLS**, using measurements for the implementations and workload. User-space location alone does not determine performance.
- **UDP blocking.** Some enterprise networks block or rate-limit UDP. Applications that support HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 can provide a TCP fallback. QUIC-only applications do not automatically acquire such a fallback.
- **Operational visibility.** Network operators lose the TCP header information they used for troubleshooting.

## A practical tuning checklist

- **Reuse connections.** Reuse can avoid setup while a connection remains valid. Idle periods can change congestion-control state.
- **Watch idle restarts.** Linux documents `tcp_slow_start_after_idle = 1` as enabling window timeout after sufficient idle time. Assess the algorithm, version and burst risk before changing it; there is no universal recommendation to disable it.
- **Check buffer limits against measured BDP** if flow control is limiting throughput. Linux socket-memory accounting and advertised windows differ; blindly raising maxima may waste memory without helping.
- **Compare congestion control and pacing configurations** under representative load, including competing traffic and latency. Do not infer a universal BBR improvement from one test.
- **Measure latency under load**, not just throughput.

## Key takeaways

- QUIC provides per-stream ordering, protected frames and separate packet-number spaces over UDP.
- Connection IDs can support eligible validated migration; shared congestion and resource constraints remain.
- CPU cost, UDP reachability and operational visibility require implementation- and path-specific assessment.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9000: QUIC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [RFC 9001: Using TLS to Secure QUIC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001)
- [RFC 9002: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002)
- [The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment — Google (SIGCOMM 2017)](https://research.google/pubs/the-quic-transport-protocol-design-and-internet-scale-deployment/)

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine features of QUIC compared with TCP plus TLS? Select all that apply.

options.text: It combines transport and TLS setup and can support eligible 0-RTT early data
options.explanation: Correct. Prior state/configuration is required for early data; rejection, replay concerns, Retry or loss can alter timing.

options.text: Its per-stream ordering avoids making one stream wait solely for missing bytes on another stream
options.explanation: Correct. Shared congestion control, flow control and application dependencies can still affect several streams.

options.text: Connection IDs can support client address changes when migration conditions are satisfied
options.explanation: Correct. Negotiated restrictions, handshake state, usable connection IDs, QUIC path validation and reachability matter; seamless success is not guaranteed.

options.text: It delivers all streams' data in one global order, like TCP
options.explanation: That would reintroduce head-of-line blocking. Ordering is per stream only.

options.text: It is implemented in the OS kernel, which makes it faster to deploy
options.explanation: QUIC can run in user-space libraries or other implementation locations. Its specification does not require a kernel implementation.

questions.workedExample: The first three describe protocol capabilities with their conditions. QUIC does not impose a single global stream delivery order, and its specification does not dictate kernel placement.

questions.prompt: Within a QUIC packet-number space, each newly sent packet gets a new increasing packet number, even when it resends stream data. Which TCP retransmission ambiguity does this remove?

options.text: Packets are smaller, because packet numbers are shorter than sequence numbers
options.explanation: Size isn't the point; QUIC packet numbers can be encoded compactly, but the real gain is unambiguous acknowledgements.

options.text: An ACK identifies which numbered packet transmission arrived, removing original-versus-retransmission ambiguity for that packet
options.explanation: Correct. Other estimation errors and spurious loss declarations remain possible; packet numbers do not make all loss detection infallible.

options.text: Data never needs to be retransmitted
options.explanation: Lost data must still be resent; it is simply sent in a new packet with a new number, with stream offsets keeping the data's position.

options.text: It allows middleboxes to reorder packets correctly
options.explanation: Packet numbers have header protection. An observer can derive Initial protection keys, so “middleboxes can never read any packet numbers” would also be too strong.

questions.workedExample: TCP reuses byte sequence numbers when resending data, so an ACK may not reveal which copy caused it; Karn’s rule or timestamps address RTT-sampling ambiguity. QUIC identifies packet transmissions separately from stream offsets, within each packet-number space. This removes that particular ambiguity. ACK delay, sampling choices and reordering still require careful recovery logic.

questions.prompt: A phone loses its old Wi-Fi path and gains a new address on 5G. Compare ordinary TCP (without MPTCP or an address-preserving tunnel) with a confirmed QUIC connection using usable connection IDs. Assume active migration is allowed and the new path passes validation and remains reachable. Which connection can continue at the transport level?

options.text: Both continue seamlessly, because the server recognises the device
options.explanation: TCP has no concept of a device; a connection is its 4-tuple. A new client IP is a different connection as far as TCP is concerned.

options.text: Both break; the application must resume the download in either case
options.explanation: Under the supplied conditions, QUIC can migrate the existing connection to the new path.

options.text: Ordinary TCP cannot move the existing connection to the new address; QUIC can continue through migration
options.explanation: Correct under the stated assumptions. QUIC still needs appropriate QUIC path validation and congestion-control handling; this does not promise no interruption.

options.text: The QUIC connection breaks but TCP continues, because TCP retransmits to the new address
options.explanation: TCP has no way to change a connection's addresses. Segments from the new IP don't match any existing connection.

questions.workedExample: Ordinary TCP identifies the connection by its endpoint addresses and ports, so the stated address change cannot simply retarget it. An application can reconnect and resume if its protocol supports that. QUIC connection IDs allow the established connection to be found from a new address; validation and path-state changes still apply. The question explicitly supplies successful migration conditions rather than assuming every network change succeeds.

lessons.title: Socket lifecycle and pending queues
lessons.summary: What each socket call does in TCP, and how the SYN and accept queues behave under load.
lessons.body:
Python's **socket API** wraps the operating system's networking calls. Similar concepts appear in other languages, but high-level runtimes, platforms and socket modes differ in their errors, buffering and lifetime rules.

This lesson follows a TCP connection through the socket calls on each side, then looks at the two kernel queues that hold connections before the application accepts them. Framing, short reads and complete servers follow in the next lessons.

## The calls and what they do in TCP

```
Server                 Client
socket()               socket()
bind(port)
listen(backlog)        connect(addr)
   SYN queue  <-- SYN ----
              --- SYN+ACK -->
   accept q   <-- ACK ----  (returns)
accept()  (returns a new socket)
recv()/send()  <------>  send()/recv()
close()        <-FIN/ACK->  close()
```

| Call | What happens in the kernel |
|---|---|
| `socket()` | Creates an endpoint; state CLOSED |
| `bind()` | Associates a local address/port, subject to reuse rules |
| `listen(n)` | State LISTEN; creates the queues |
| `connect()` | Ordinary blocking TCP: initiates setup, then succeeds or fails; non-blocking mode differs |
| `accept()` | Returns a new connected socket from pending connections |
| `close()` | Releases this socket reference; final closure can initiate FIN or an abort, depending on state/options |

Two points surprise people:

- **`accept()` does not perform the handshake.** The kernel completes handshakes on its own, whether or not the application is calling `accept()`. In ordinary TCP it dequeues a completed connection and returns a **new** socket; the peer may already have sent FIN before acceptance. Fast Open can allow acceptance before the normal handshake finishes. The listener remains available.
- **Ordinary blocking `connect()` success means the client-side handshake progressed successfully**, not that the server application accepted you or processed data. Queue overflow can leave the server still waiting to complete its side.

## The backlog and the two queues

A useful Linux model distinguishes two kinds of pending state (SYN cookies can avoid allocating an entry per SYN):

1. The **SYN queue**: half-open connections waiting for the final ACK.
2. The **accept queue**: completed connections waiting for `accept()`.

The `backlog` argument to `listen()` sets the size of the **accept queue**, capped by `net.core.somaxconn` (4,096 by default since Linux 5.4; 128 before).

If the application is too slow to accept and that queue fills, one Linux path with `tcp_abort_on_overflow = 0` can **ignore** the client's final ACK; other overload paths can drop SYNs. The client thinks it's connected and may send its request; the server retransmits SYN+ACK and the connection completes later, or not. The symptom is clients seeing occasional multi-second delays on connect or first request. `nstat` shows `TcpExtListenOverflows` climbing.

> [!tip] Investigate queue overload
> Arrival bursts, slow acceptance, resource limits and backlog configuration can all contribute. Inspect application scheduling and queue/counter measurements. A growing overflow counter does not by itself identify a single cause or prove one packet-level sequence.

## Key takeaways

- The kernel can progress an ordinary TCP handshake before the application accepts it.
- Acceptance returns a separate connected socket while the listener remains available.
- Linux pending queues, caps and overflow paths need version/configuration-aware diagnosis.

## Further reading

- [Python socket module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html)
- [SYN packet handling in the wild — Cloudflare blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/syn-packet-handling-in-the-wild/)
- [Beej's Guide to Network Programming](https://beej.us/guide/bgnet/)

questions.prompt: An ordinary Linux TCP listener has room in its pending queues, the path is working, and no Fast Open is in use. Its process is stopped in a debugger after listen(128), before accept(). Can a client’s blocking connect() succeed?

options.text: connect() succeeds: the kernel completes the handshake and queues the connection for accept()
options.explanation: Correct. Handshakes are handled by the kernel. The connection sits in the accept queue, and the client can even send data, which waits in the server's receive buffer.

options.text: connect() blocks until the server calls accept()
options.explanation: The kernel can perform the ordinary TCP handshake without the application accepting. The peer may even half-close before the server eventually accepts.

options.text: connect() fails with ConnectionRefusedError
options.explanation: Refusal (RST) happens when nothing is listening. A socket in LISTEN accepts handshakes even when its process is stuck.

options.text: connect() times out after about two minutes
options.explanation: The supplied conditions do not require waiting for acceptance or a timeout. Timeout durations are configuration-dependent.

questions.workedExample: The kernel listener can process SYN and ACK traffic while the application is paused. The client can complete its local handshake and queue data before the server calls accept(). The requested backlog is subject to platform limits and does not establish an exact universal 128-connection failure threshold.

questions.prompt: A Linux service shows rising TcpExtListenOverflows and occasional delayed connection setup or first requests. With tcp_abort_on_overflow = 0, which explanation is consistent with these observations and should be investigated using captures and queue measurements?

options.text: The accept queue is overloaded; some handshakes may be deferred or dropped while the listener catches up
options.explanation: Correct. One overflow path ignores the final ACK and can recover after SYN+ACK retransmission. Other paths and causes exist; this counter alone does not prove that exact trace.

options.text: A SYN flood is filling the SYN queue
options.explanation: A SYN-queue problem alone is not established by this accept-overflow counter. Attack traffic can still contribute to several types of overload, so do not exclude it solely from one counter.

options.text: Nagle's algorithm is delaying the first request
options.explanation: Nagle is not the mechanism counted by a listen-queue overflow counter. Its delay is not universally bounded to a fixed millisecond range.

options.text: TIME_WAIT sockets are blocking new connections
options.explanation: TIME_WAIT on the server's port doesn't block new connections from different client tuples, and isn't counted by ListenOverflows.

questions.workedExample: Inspect backlog limits, arrival bursts, acceptance rate, blocked workers and resource limits. Linux can ignore a final ACK on an overflow path when abort-on-overflow is disabled, while the client already believes setup succeeded. Retries can then add delay, but exact timing and behaviour require capture/configuration evidence. A larger backlog absorbs some bursts; it does not fix sustained service-capacity shortfalls.
