lessons.title: Byte streams and message framing
lessons.summary: Why TCP does not keep your send() boundaries, and the framing rules applications use instead.
lessons.body:
## A stream has no message boundaries

TCP delivers a **byte stream**. It does not preserve the boundaries of your `send()` calls:

```
client: send(b"hello")
client: send(b"world")

server recv(1024) may return:
  b"helloworld"         (coalesced)
  b"hel", then b"loworld" (split)
  b"hello", then b"world"
```

All three are correct TCP behaviour. Nagle, segmentation, retransmission and the timing of `recv()` calls all affect where the cuts fall. A one-read-per-message assumption can fail even on localhost; a passing local test does not establish framing correctness.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Dictating over a crackly phone without punctuation
> You read two sentences down the phone to someone writing them down. They hear every word in order, but if you never say "full stop", they cannot tell where one sentence ends and the next begins, and they may have written half a sentence when you pause.
>
> **How it maps:** The words arriving in order are TCP's ordered byte stream; your pauses are `send()` calls, which the listener cannot see; each `recv()` is them writing down whatever they have heard so far. Saying "full stop" is a delimiter, and announcing "the next sentence has twelve words" is a length prefix.
>
> **Where it stops:** A person can guess sentence breaks from meaning, but a program cannot: without an explicit rule it will read exactly what arrived, which might be one and a half messages.

Protocols that distinguish messages need **framing**. A single stream-to-EOF transfer can use EOF as its boundary:

- **Length prefix**: send a fixed-size length, then that many bytes. For example, gRPC has its own message-length prefix inside HTTP/2 DATA frames; the HTTP/2 frame header is a separate framing layer.
- **Delimiter**: end each message with a marker, such as `\r\n` in SMTP and in HTTP/1.1 headers. The receiver buffers until it finds one.
- **Protocol-defined body rules**: HTTP/1.1 uses status/method rules, `Content-Length`, chunked encoding, or connection closure as applicable; not every response has a body.

## Key takeaways

- TCP preserves byte order rather than application write boundaries.
- A receiver may observe a send split across reads or several sends combined.
- Length prefixes, delimiters and protocol-defined EOF/body rules supply message framing.

## Further reading

- [Socket Programming HOWTO — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sockets.html)
- [Python socket module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html)

questions.prompt: Why does a TCP application that needs to distinguish messages need a framing rule, such as a length prefix, delimiter or a defined EOF boundary?

options.text: Because TCP may reorder bytes, and framing puts them back in order
options.explanation: TCP already guarantees in-order delivery. Framing is about where messages begin and end, not order.

options.text: Because TCP limits each send() to one MSS
options.explanation: send() is not restricted to one MSS; it can accept more, or only part of the supplied buffer. Segmentation is separate from application framing.

options.text: Because TCP is a byte stream and doesn't preserve the boundaries of send() calls
options.explanation: Correct. The receiver may get two messages in one recv() or half a message, so it needs a rule for finding message boundaries.

options.text: Because framing is needed to compute TCP's checksum
options.explanation: TCP checksums cover segments, independently of application message framing. They may be computed by the protocol stack or hardware offload; a kernel implementation is not required.

questions.workedExample: TCP preserves byte order but not write boundaries. A receiver may obtain part of a message or several messages in one read. A protocol must define how to recognise its boundaries, which may include EOF. Ordinary UDP preserves the boundary of each delivered datagram, but datagrams can be lost, duplicated or truncated by an undersized receive buffer.

questions.prompt: On a fresh TCP stream with no other reader, a client successfully sends b"hello" then b"world". No local receive shutdown or connection failure occurs. Which results could the server’s first recv(1024) return? Select all that apply.

options.text: `b"helloworld"`
options.explanation: Possible. Both writes may arrive (or be coalesced into one segment) before the server reads.

options.text: `b"hel"`
options.explanation: Possible. recv() returns whatever has arrived so far, which may be a fragment of the first write.

options.text: `b"hello"`
options.explanation: Possible, and common in testing, which is why the bug of assuming it is easy to miss.

options.text: `b"world"`
options.explanation: Impossible. TCP delivers bytes in order, so the first bytes returned must start with "h".

options.text: `b"worldhello"`
options.explanation: Impossible. Reordering is never visible through a TCP socket.

questions.workedExample:
TCP delivers received stream bytes in order; it does not preserve write boundaries or promise that a connection can never fail.

1. The byte stream is `helloworld`.
2. The first `recv()` returns some non-empty **prefix** of the bytes that have arrived: `h`, `hel`, `hello`, `hellowor`, `helloworld`...
3. Anything that doesn't start at the first byte (`world`, `worldhello`) is impossible.

So A, B and C are possible.

lessons.title: Short I/O, EOF and operation deadlines
lessons.summary: Short reads, partial writes, end of stream and timeouts: the rules for using socket calls correctly.
lessons.body:
## Partial reads, partial writes and EOF

Three rules for using the calls correctly:

1. For a positive `n`, ordinary blocking **`recv(n)` returns at most n bytes**. Short reads are allowed. Flags, low-water settings, timeouts and errors can change when it returns; loop for a specified length.
2. **`send()` may send only part of the buffer**, returning the count it accepted, for example because of limited buffer capacity. Python's `sendall()` handles partial writes on blocking sockets, but may raise; success means local acceptance, not peer processing.
3. With a positive read size and no local receive shutdown, **`recv()` returning `b""` indicates end of stream** after received bytes have been consumed: the peer closed its sending direction. It is not an error and not "no data yet". If you don't treat it as the end, you'll spin forever on a closed connection.

Error conditions show up as exceptions:

| Python exception | Usual meaning |
|---|---|
| `ConnectionRefusedError` | RST in reply to SYN |
| `ConnectionResetError` | Peer sent RST mid-connection |
| `BrokenPipeError` | Writing to a stream no longer usable for sending; peer half-close alone need not cause it |
| `TimeoutError` / `socket.timeout` | An operation exceeded its applicable timeout; `sendall()` has an overall timeout |

Choose operation timeouts and application deadlines. A silent peer can otherwise leave a blocking read waiting indefinitely. Linux’s documented default keepalive idle interval is 7,200 seconds when keepalive is enabled, but applications and configuration can change it. Keepalive is not a substitute for a request deadline.

## Key takeaways

- Positive-length reads may be short and sends may accept only part of a buffer.
- Empty bytes indicate stream EOF under the stated socket conditions, not temporary lack of data.
- Operation timeouts, total request deadlines and application acknowledgements solve different problems.

## Further reading

- [Python socket module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html)
- [Socket Programming HOWTO — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sockets.html)

questions.prompt: On a blocking TCP socket with no local receive shutdown, recv(4096) returns b"" after all preceding data has been consumed. What does this indicate?

options.text: No data has arrived yet; call recv() again shortly
options.explanation: A blocking recv() waits until data arrives; it never returns empty just because nothing is there yet. (A non-blocking socket raises BlockingIOError instead.)

options.text: The peer has closed its sending side (sent FIN); there will be no more data
options.explanation: Correct. An empty read is end-of-stream. Your code should stop reading and, usually, close the socket.

options.text: The peer sent an RST
options.explanation: An RST surfaces as an exception, ConnectionResetError, not as an empty read.

options.text: The receive buffer is full
options.explanation: A full buffer means there's plenty to read; recv() would return data immediately.

questions.workedExample: For this positive-length read, an empty result indicates end of the peer’s sending stream. Stop waiting for further input. A half-closed connection may still be usable for sending a response; then close or shut down according to the protocol. Forgetting EOF handling can create a busy loop, but the exact TCP state also depends on local shutdown history.

lessons.title: A bounded length-prefixed TCP service
lessons.summary: A small threaded server that frames messages with a four-byte length prefix and bounds their size.
lessons.body:
## A length-prefixed server with threads

First, framing helpers. `recv_exact` loops until it has exactly `n` bytes, and treats EOF in the middle as an error:

```python
import socket, struct, threading

MAX_MSG = 1024 * 1024  # teaching limit

def recv_exact(sock, n):
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid length")
    buf = bytearray()
    while len(buf) < n:
        # Request only the missing suffix.
        chunk = sock.recv(n - len(buf))
        if not chunk:
            # EOF before all requested
            # bytes.
            raise EOFError
        buf += chunk
    return bytes(buf)

def recv_msg(sock):
    hdr = recv_exact(sock, 4)
    # Decode an unsigned big-endian length.
    (n,) = struct.unpack("!I", hdr)
    # Reject oversized claims before reads.
    if n > MAX_MSG:
        raise ValueError("too large")
    return recv_exact(sock, n)

def send_msg(sock, data):
    if len(data) > MAX_MSG:
        raise ValueError("too large")
    hdr = struct.pack("!I", len(data))
    # Retry partial writes of prefix + body.
    sock.sendall(hdr + data)
```

`"!I"` is a 4-byte unsigned integer in network byte order (big-endian). Big-endian means the first byte on the wire is the most significant, so the receiver rebuilds the length like this:

```formula reference
n = b_0 × 2^24 + b_1 × 2^16
  + b_2 × 2^8 + b_3
where
n: the message length the prefix encodes, in bytes
b_0: the first byte received (most significant), 0 to 255
b_1: the second byte
b_2: the third byte
b_3: the fourth byte (least significant)
In words: each prefix byte is worth 256 times the byte after it, so the bytes 00 00 01 00 mean 256.
```

Four bytes can claim a length of up to about 4 GiB (4,294,967,295 bytes). That is why `recv_msg` checks the decoded length against `MAX_MSG` (1 MiB here) **before** reading the body: otherwise a single malformed or hostile header could make the server try to read and buffer gigabytes.

Combining header and body avoids an application-created pause between two small writes, but one `sendall()` is not one packet and cannot guarantee freedom from Nagle, queueing or other delays.

Then the server, one thread per connection:

```python
def handle(conn, addr):
    with conn:
        conn.settimeout(5)
        try:
            while True:
                msg = recv_msg(conn)
                # Reply only to a complete
                # message.
                send_msg(conn, msg.upper())
        except (EOFError, OSError,
                ValueError):
            pass  # toy policy: close

srv = socket.create_server(
    ("127.0.0.1", 9000), backlog=128)
while True:
    conn, addr = srv.accept()
    # Each client owns a separate socket.
    threading.Thread(target=handle,
                     args=(conn, addr),
                     daemon=True).start()
```

And a client:

```python
with socket.create_connection(
        ("127.0.0.1", 9000),
        timeout=5) as s:
    s.settimeout(5)
    send_msg(s, b"hello")
    print(recv_msg(s))   # b'HELLO'
```

Details that make this correct:

- `with conn:` closes this socket when the handler exits. It cannot force a handler that never exits to finish; duplicated references and wrappers also affect lifetime.
- The helpers cap each body at 1 MiB. The handler has a per-operation timeout, not a total-message deadline: a trickling peer can keep a message in progress. Production code needs total deadlines, connection/thread limits and a deliberate error policy.
- `socket.create_server` sets **`SO_REUSEADDR`** on POSIX systems. Without suitable reuse settings, retained connection state can stop the port being bound again immediately. This is not an inevitable outcome of every restart; address, platform and old/new socket options matter.

> [!note] SO_REUSEADDR vs SO_REUSEPORT
> `SO_REUSEADDR` relaxes platform-specific bind rules; it does not grant arbitrary sharing with an active listener. Linux generally requires the reuse option on both the previous and new sockets for the relevant reuse case. `SO_REUSEPORT` (Linux 3.9+) supports multiple eligible listeners at the same address/port, each with its own queue. Sockets must set it before binding; Linux requires matching effective user IDs. Default selection and optional BPF policies do not guarantee perfectly balanced work.

## Key takeaways

- Loop until the requested header/body length is assembled and cap claimed body sizes.
- Network byte order makes the most significant prefix byte arrive first.
- Thread lifetimes, socket reuse rules and per-operation timeouts require explicit production policies.

## Further reading

- [Python socket module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html)
- [Socket Programming HOWTO — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sockets.html)

questions.prompt: On a POSIX system, diagnostics show that retained TIME_WAIT connections prevent a new listener binding the port immediately, with no competing listener. Which option should a restartable server configure before bind(), subject to that platform’s old/new socket reuse rules?

options.text: The old process is still running; kill it with kill -9
options.explanation: The question says nothing is listening. The port is held by connection state, not by a process.

options.text: Port 8080 is reserved for root; run the server as root
options.explanation: This is an address-reuse problem, not a permission error. Privileged-port thresholds are platform/configuration-dependent.

options.text: SO_REUSEADDR; Python socket.create_server enables it on POSIX
options.explanation: Correct. Configure appropriate reuse before binding. On Linux the relevant reuse case generally requires it on both the old and new sockets; exact rules differ across systems.

options.text: The ephemeral port range has been exhausted
options.explanation: Exhaustion of automatically selected local ports is a different failure mode. Here the supplied diagnostics identify retained TIME_WAIT state affecting an explicit bind; an existing conflicting allocation can also matter when a chosen fixed port overlaps the automatic range.

questions.workedExample:
TIME_WAIT retains TCP state after orderly closure and can stop the port being bound again. SO_REUSEADDR relaxes relevant address-reuse checks, subject to platform rules; it does not permit arbitrary sharing with an active listener. Set it before bind(), and configure the original listener appropriately too.

```python
s = socket.socket()
# Configure before binding the port.
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,
             socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8080))
```

The caller must close s when finished. Port reuse does not mean new connections necessarily have different tuples; TCP’s retained state and sequence rules still matter.

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's `recv_msg`, a peer sends these 10 bytes in one segment:

```
00 00 00 03 61 62 63 64 65 66
```

(0x61 to 0x66 are `a` to `f`.) What does the first `recv_msg(sock)` call return?

options.text: `b"abcdef"`
options.explanation: The header says the body is 3 bytes. recv_exact asks for exactly 3, so the last three stay in the buffer for the next call.

options.text: `b"abc"`
options.explanation: Correct. The header 00 00 00 03 decodes as 3, so recv_exact(sock, 3) returns b"abc". The bytes def remain unread.

options.text: `b"\x00\x00\x00\x03abcdef"`
options.explanation: recv_msg strips the 4-byte header and uses it as a length; it doesn't return it.

options.text: It raises EOFError because the message is incomplete
options.explanation: The 3-byte body is complete. EOFError only occurs if the peer closes before enough bytes arrive.

questions.workedExample:
1. `recv_exact(sock, 4)` reads `00 00 00 03`.
2. `struct.unpack("!I", ...)` reads a big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer. Big-endian puts the most significant byte first, so three zero bytes followed by `03` decode as 3.
3. 3 is below `MAX_MSG`, so `recv_exact(sock, 3)` reads `61 62 63` = `b"abc"`.
4. `64 65 66` (`def`) remains in the socket buffer. The **next** `recv_msg` would take those three bytes plus one more as its header: an incomplete next header. It could be malformed input or part of a later message; the three bytes alone do not prove the peer uses another protocol. The lesson's size limit rejects an oversized decoded next length.

questions.prompt: An Nginx-style server runs 8 worker processes. In design A they all accept from one shared listening socket. In design B each worker opens its own listening socket on port 443 with `SO_REUSEPORT`. What is the main effect of design B on Linux?

options.text: The kernel selects among separate eligible listening sockets, each with its own accept queue, which can reduce shared-listener contention
options.explanation: Correct. Linux’s default selection uses flow-related hashing, but optional BPF policies and implementation details vary. Neither perfect balancing nor removal of all locking is guaranteed.

options.text: It lets the server bind port 443 while old connections are in TIME_WAIT
options.explanation: That's what SO_REUSEADDR does. SO_REUSEPORT is about multiple simultaneous listeners.

options.text: Each worker receives a copy of every incoming connection
options.explanation: A connection is delivered to exactly one of the listening sockets; copying would make no sense for TCP.

options.text: It allows more than 65,535 connections to port 443
options.explanation: One listening socket can already have far more connections than that; connections are told apart by the client's address and port.

questions.workedExample: With one shared listener, workers take connections from one accept queue. An eligible SO_REUSEPORT group has separate listeners and queues; set the option before bind() and satisfy Linux’s effective-UID and binding requirements. Selection can distribute new connections without every worker sharing one accept queue. A stalled worker can still accumulate work, and measured workload balance is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt:
This code works in local tests but occasionally raises `struct.error: unpack requires a buffer of 4 bytes` in production. Why?

```python
# BUG: one read may return <4 bytes.
hdr = sock.recv(4)
(n,) = struct.unpack("!I", hdr)
body = sock.recv(n)
```

options.text: Network byte order is little-endian, so `!I` is wrong
options.explanation: Network byte order is big-endian, which is exactly what `!` means. The format is fine.

options.text: recv(4) can return fewer than 4 bytes, for example when the header is split across segments
options.explanation: Correct. recv(n) returns up to n bytes, whatever is available. The fix is a recv_exact loop. The same bug also affects `sock.recv(n)` for the body.

options.text: The sender's Nagle algorithm drops the header
options.explanation: Nagle may delay or coalesce data, but it never drops bytes.

options.text: recv() must always be called with a buffer of at least 4,096 bytes
options.explanation: A positive receive size smaller than 4,096 is valid. The bug is assuming the result always fills the requested length.

questions.workedExample:
1. `recv(4)` means 'give me **at most** 4 bytes'.
2. A local test may happen to return the complete header, but short reads are possible even on localhost.
3. Over a real network, the 4-byte header may straddle two segments, or the peer may write it in pieces. Then `recv(4)` returns, say, 2 bytes, and `unpack` fails.
4. `recv(n)` for the body has the same flaw, but fails silently by returning a short body.
5. Fix: use the lesson’s recv_exact and MAX_MSG, handling EOF/errors and bounding the decoded size before reading the body.

```python
# Assemble the entire length prefix.
hdr = recv_exact(sock, 4)
(n,) = struct.unpack("!I", hdr)
# Bound allocation/read work first.
if n > MAX_MSG:
    raise ValueError("too large")
body = recv_exact(sock, n)
```

lessons.title: Readiness pitfalls and asyncio backpressure
lessons.summary: Serving many connections from one thread with readiness APIs or asyncio, and why backpressure still matters.
lessons.body:
## Scaling: threads versus an event loop

A thread per connection is simple, but stack reservations, task limits and scheduling costs constrain scale. Exact limits and stack sizes depend on the runtime and platform. Many mostly idle connections motivate multiplexing rather than one native thread each.

The alternative is **non-blocking sockets** and a **readiness API**: `select`/`poll`, `epoll` (Linux) or `kqueue` (BSD, macOS). Availability differs by platform: Python exposes `poll` on Unix, while Windows `select` handles sockets only. In the usual scanning-cost model, `select` scales with the highest descriptor number and `poll` with the number of supplied descriptors. One thread asks the kernel "which of these sockets can I read or write without blocking?" and handles only those. Python's `selectors` module chooses an available backend according to its platform policy. Readiness can become stale: operations on non-blocking sockets must still handle `BlockingIOError`.

**Deliberately faulty debugging example:** the next loop ignores partial writes and can exit on an unhandled would-block error. It is the subject of this unit’s partial-write quiz, not a correct echo-server template:

```python
import selectors, socket

EV = selectors.EVENT_READ
sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()
srv = socket.create_server(
    ("127.0.0.1", 9001))
srv.setblocking(False)
sel.register(srv, EV)

while True:
    for key, _ in sel.select():
        s = key.fileobj
        if s is srv:
            conn, _ = srv.accept()
            conn.setblocking(False)
            sel.register(conn, EV)
            continue
        try:
            data = s.recv(4096)
        except ConnectionError:
            data = b""
        if data:
            # BUG: the unsent suffix is
            # lost.
            s.send(data)  # may be partial
        else:
            # Remove this endpoint from the
            # loop.
            sel.unregister(s)
            s.close()
```

This loop can lose echo bytes or terminate. Correct readiness handling requires partial-write accounting, would-block/error handling for accept/read/write, bounded per-connection output queues, read backpressure, cleanup and half-close handling. Enable write interest only while output is pending and flush pending output before closing after input EOF. Frameworks provide parts of this machinery, but applications must still choose limits, framing and deadlines.

`asyncio` gives the same event-loop efficiency with sequential-looking code:

```python
import asyncio

async def handle(reader, writer):
    try:
        while True:
            data = await reader.read(4096)
            if not data:
                break
            # Queue the transformed reply.
            writer.write(data.upper())
            # Wait for transport buffer
            # capacity.
            await writer.drain()
    except ConnectionError:
        pass
    finally:
        writer.close()
        try:
            await writer.wait_closed()
        except ConnectionError:
            pass

async def main():
    srv = await asyncio.start_server(
        handle, "127.0.0.1", 9002)
    async with srv:
        await srv.serve_forever()

asyncio.run(main())
```

`writer.drain()` cooperates with the transport’s high/low watermarks: after writing is paused at the high watermark, it waits for the buffer to drain to the low watermark. It does not wait for a peer application acknowledgment. Slow readers, congestion or limited path capacity can cause backpressure; a zero receive window is not required. This echo sample has cleanup but still needs application deadlines and connection/resource limits for deployment.

## Key takeaways

- A readiness notification does not remove partial-write or would-block handling requirements.
- The selector loop is deliberately faulty and must not be copied as a correct server.
- asyncio drain cooperates with transport buffer watermarks; it does not acknowledge peer application processing.

## Further reading

- [Python selectors module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/selectors.html)
- [The C10K problem — Dan Kegel](http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html)
- [Python socket module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html)

questions.prompt: A thread-per-connection Python server handles 50 clients well. You need to hold 50,000 mostly idle WebSocket-style connections. Why is the threaded design likely to struggle, and what's the standard alternative?

options.text: Python threads can't call recv(); use processes instead
options.explanation: Threads can call recv(); in CPython’s usual GIL-enabled build, blocking socket I/O releases the GIL. Replacing each native thread with a process adds separate process-management costs and does not remove the need to measure resource limits.

options.text: TCP limits a server to 65,535 connections per port
options.explanation: A listener can serve more than 65,535 connections when peer endpoint tuples differ sufficiently. Resource and tuple limits still apply.

options.text: Each thread needs its own listening port
options.explanation: All connections are accepted from one listening socket; each thread only uses its accepted socket.

options.text: Native threads have stack and scheduling costs; a multiplexed runtime can serve many idle sockets with fewer threads
options.explanation: Correct. Backend and runtime details vary; a benchmark and resource limits determine actual capacity.

questions.workedExample: One native thread per connection adds stack reservations, task limits and scheduling overhead. A readiness or completion-based runtime can multiplex many waiting operations onto fewer threads. Connections still consume kernel buffers, application state, descriptors and runtime tasks. No fixed 50,000-connection capacity follows from choosing an event loop.

questions.prompt: Consider the lesson's `selectors` echo server, which calls `s.send(data)` once on a non-blocking socket. A client sends a lot of data quickly but reads its replies very slowly. Which problems can occur? Select all that apply.

options.text: send() may accept only part of `data`, and the rest is silently lost from the echo
options.explanation: Correct. send() on a non-blocking socket returns how many bytes it took; the code ignores the return value, so any remainder is never sent.

options.text: send() may raise BlockingIOError when the socket's send buffer is completely full
options.explanation: Correct. Once the slow client's receive window and our send buffer are full, a send on a non-blocking socket can't accept anything, and the code doesn't catch it, so the loop crashes.

options.text: The send call on the non-blocking socket itself waits for the slow client to read
options.explanation: False. It returns a count or an error rather than waiting for writability. However, an unhandled exception can terminate this toy loop and interrupt service for every client.

options.text: Correct handling needs retained unsent output and write readiness, plus queue bounds, read backpressure and error handling
options.explanation: Correct. Account for partial writes and handle would-block, disconnection and cleanup; an unbounded output buffer merely moves the resource problem.

options.text: Switching to sendall() on the non-blocking socket fully solves it
options.explanation: On a non-blocking socket, sendall() can still raise BlockingIOError partway through, leaving an unknown amount sent. It doesn't replace proper output buffering.

questions.workedExample: The deliberately faulty loop ignores send()’s partial count and does not handle would-block. It can lose bytes or terminate. A call on a non-blocking socket does not wait for the slow peer, but loop termination affects all clients. Retain pending output, ask for write-readiness notifications only while needed, bound queues and stop reading when output pressure is high. Handle stale readiness for accept/read/write and flush pending output on input half-close. sendall() alone does not solve buffering for non-blocking sockets.

questions.prompt: In the asyncio echo example, suppose the peer keeps uploading but never reads responses. With no output-size policy or total deadline added, what risk is introduced by deleting await writer.drain()?

options.text: Nothing; asyncio writes everything immediately
options.explanation: write() may send immediately or buffer unsent data. It does not wait for the receiving application to consume it.

options.text: The server crashes with BrokenPipeError immediately
options.explanation: Not reading replies does not itself require an immediate BrokenPipeError. Queued output can grow while the connection remains usable; unrelated failures or later endpoint closure are still possible.

options.text: TCP drops the responses, and the client receives them later via retransmission
options.explanation: Retransmission does not replace application backpressure. Data can accumulate in the asyncio transport’s output buffer.

options.text: Unsent output can grow excessively because the coroutine no longer waits for the transport’s backpressure
options.explanation: Correct. drain() waits when writing is paused at the high watermark until the buffer drains to the low watermark. Other failures or limits may stop growth; unlimited growth is a risk, not an inevitable trace.

questions.workedExample: If incoming data continues while output cannot drain, write() can accumulate unsent output in user space. drain() makes the coroutine cooperate with transport flow control, indirectly slowing further reads. Its watermarks concern the transport buffer, not a direct test for a zero TCP receive window. Removing it risks memory exhaustion; exact growth and termination depend on the runtime, peer and other limits.
